PROCEEDINGS
This is an interview with Benny Carter, conducted by Marl Berger as part of the oral jazz history program of the Smithsonian Institution. We are in Princeton, and this is October 13, 1976.
Benny, to begin at the beginning, let's just ask where and when you were born.
I was born in New York City on August 8, 1907.
How did you feel?
I felt pretty good at the time!
Okay.
But I feel much better now.
All right. When did you begin to get interested in music as nearly as you can remember?

Well, as nearly as I can remember, it must have been about at the age of 10. And my mother played piano, not professionally, of course -- but she played in church occasionally, and she gave me some piano lessons at home.

And following that, my sister -- who had been studying piano -- she gave me some piano lessons. And following that when she could stand me no longer, I took some lessons from the teacher from whom she had been taught.
Do you remember that her teacher's name?
No, I don't.
That was a piano teacher.
Yes.
And that must have been -- when? About 1917 when you were about 10, or maybe a little bit later?
Well, about ten. Well, Actually, when I went to the piano teacher, it was about a year later.
So it was about 1918.
When you were about 11.
Yes, something like that, yes.
By the way, where in New York were you born and where did you spend your early years?

Well, I was born in what was at that time called Sloane's Hospital for Women at, I believe, it that was at 60th 66th Street and Amsterdam Avenue. I lived at 246 West 63rd Street, which was just east of West End Avenue -- between West End and Amsterdam. And that's where I spent my early years.
Yeah. Was that the area called San Juan Hill?
That was. San Juan Hill.
It was not Hell's Kitchen, was it?
No. Hell's Kitchen was down, I believe, in the 40's -- in the upper 40's, south of there.
What kind of a neighborhood would you say it was in whatever terms you remember?

Well, it was what we would call, even now -- and even then -- a ghetto, you know. Not the worst ghetto. We weren't in too bad a shape. We weren't poverty stricken. I can't remember ever having to miss a meal.

But it was kind of a rough neighborhood, and, really -- not too rough. It was mostly rough -- leaving the neighborhood, going to school and back, you know, because we had to literally fight our way to school and back. I mean, usually the youngsters -- my contemporaries -- we'd have to meet on the corner and go to school together, you know?
To get mutual protection?
Mutual protection, that's right ... collective.

Right. In your schooling, since you mentioned this mutual protection that you needed to have in order to go to school, how did -- or how far did you go, what kind of a school boy were you, did you like to go to school, did you try to study music at school?
Well, I did like school, yes, and I guess I played about as much hookey as, you know, many of the other young guys did at that time. At about the age of
14, I believe it was, would I have been in the 7th grade then?
Yes, 7th or 8th grade.

Yeah. Just before I would have graduated from elementary, or would they call it grammar school? I don't know what they call it now. I got in to a fight with another one of the pupils, and a particular teacher took his side and gave me a kick, almost, down a flight of steps because we got to fighting on the steps, going downstairs, and when the teacher kicked me -- and he kicked me in the back -- I don't yet know why; I guess he just didn't like me -- I fell to the next landing and got up and socked it to him, and I was expelled from school.
And I guess in those days, you didn't have to go to a continuation school or anything.
I don't remember exactly, but ... I don't know. I remember too well what happened. I became so absorbed in music following that, and then I really just got ...
But at that time, for a kid of that age, you were deeply involved in music, weren't you?
Yes. I had gotten an instrument.
You had already bought an instrument?
Yes, uh huh.
What was that instrument?

Well, the instrument that I had at that particular time was a saxophone, although I had started with a trumpet -- because I had given up on the piano. I sort of felt that I wanted to play a wind instrument, and the instrument I wanted to play was really the trumpet. I had a cousin whose name was Cuban Bennett, from Macdonald, Pennsylvania -- and he was a very, very fine trumpet player.
Had you heard him?
Oh yes.
Or had you just heard about him?

No, I had heard him. I had gone to school in Macdonald, Pennsylvania, I guess, when I was probably between 11 and 12 or something -- for about a year there. And he was probably, oh, how old? He was some years older than I was.
Maybe 10 or so years.
Yeah, maybe that much -- maybe as much as 10 years older. And I was a great fan of Bubba Miley, who lived just around the corner from me, and he was a professional musician already at that time.
That impelled you to try the trumpet first?

That did impel me to try the trumpet first, and I went and bought a trumpet, which I paid for at $1 a week for 33 weeks, I remember that -- and I earned the money by working after school at, you know, a tailor
shop, a cleaners and dyers and laundry combination, and making after school deliveries.
And at the end of this 33rd week when I went to pick up the trumpet, I went home Saturday evening, and I figured that by Monday, you know, I'd have a job playing with somebody, and ...
So you didn't get the use of the trumpet until you had paid it all off?
Oh, that's right. It was sort of what we call now a layaway plan. Right?
Yeah. That's not exactly the installment plan?
No. No. I mean, because it's not play while you pay, or pay while you play, no. I didn't get it until I paid the $33 off.
And then you got the trumpet. How did it go?

Well, it really didn't. I thought, you know, you look up at musicians up on a bandstand, and they're playing and it all looks so easy, so effortless, and it just wasn't like that. Come Monday, after that Saturday, I gave up. I had been advised by a friend in the neighborhood named Harold Proctor -- who also played the saxophone -- that maybe if I were to go and get a saxophone, it would be easier than the trumpet. I had also, by this time, been hearing saxophonist
named Frankie Trumbauer Trombar on record, and I liked what he was doing.

So, I went and got the saxophone. The interesting thing about that -- the motivation, also, was that Hal Harold said that he would help me with it, and you know, at the time no one was helping me with the trumpet; I had talked to Bubba Bubber Miley about it, but Hal Harold said if you get the saxophone, he said, it'll be easier and I can help you.

Which he did help me. It wasn't too much easier, because nothing like that is easy until you really study it, you know, to a certain degree. After which I studied with him for a while -- and when I say a while, it was quite a short while, because he didn't read music, but he could show me things about the instrument, you know? * see p 63, not whom for spelling

And then I went to a teacher named Michael -- what was his first name? Eugene. Yes. And I studied with him for a while; he also had 2 sons who were fine musicians -- Otto and Gene Jr. After studying with him a while, he turned me over -- well, at the beginning, he turned me over to who was his star pupil, Rudy Powell, who was a very fine musician. Rudy had also played violin.

Then after I studied with Michael a while -- I don't remember how long -- I went to a teacher named Arthur Reeves, with whom I studied for, oh, maybe a year or more -- and he was a very, very fine saxophone player. I tried to develop the sound that he was getting because the sound that he got was great.
Excuse me. What kind of playing did he do? Was he a performing musician or was he ...

He was a performing musician and a singer. He had his own group, that he was a teacher -- he wasn't really what you would call a jazz saxophone player. He was mostly, I guess what you would call a melodist, you know? But he was a fine teacher ... he was a fine teacher, and with him the emphasis was on sound and quality of tone, you know, and intonation.
At this time, you were about how old? By the time, let's say, you were in the middle of the work with Arthur Reeves?
Oh, this had to be about ... gee, probably coming up around 1920, or later.
So you were about 14? it had to be 1914?
About 1920 or '22, I think. I was about 14 or 15, yes.
Right. And by this time when you were through with Reeves, or when you stopped going to him, presumably, you had some control of the instrument?
Yes, some. Yes, right. I started getting some jobs around, the first of which I remember for which I was paid. Of course, I used to go around and sit in, as we did in those days.
Right.
And the first job for which I was

paid was, oh, a job at a place called Connors Inn on 135th Street, between Lenox Avenue and 5th Avenue, and it happened that something happened with the group with which Bubber Miley was playing, and the saxophone player couldn't show up or something, and Bubber took me along to play the gig.
You were both still living on West 63rd Street?
Yeah, Bubber I believe was living on 62nd.
Right.

Just around the corner, yeah. And he took me to play this job, for which I was paid $1.25 -- and in Rex Stewart's book, I think that Rex said that the man paid me another $1.25 not to come back! I don't remember, but anyway, I started playing professionally, I guess you'd call it, some time after that.
Right. So that was, again, at about the age of 15?
Yes, about 15. Maybe even later. Maybe I was 16 or something, yeah.
But when you began sitting in without pay, that was in Harlem clubs mostly?
Oh yes. Oh yes. Completely.
Do you remember some of the bands that you played, and that you sat in with?
Well, it was really -- you'd go in a
place where maybe they'd even have just a piano and drums, you know?
Yes.

I do remember very well that Count Basie was playing at a place where he just played with a drummer. And he was very, very kind to me. I used to go in and sit in with him. I used to go in and sit in with Willie "the Lion" Smith, who also played with just a piano and a drummer.

And then one of the jobs that I had in the earliest, was with Willie "the Lion" Smith when he added me to his duo to make a trio. Piano, drums and saxophone. And I must say, I certainly learned a lot from him.
Uh huh.

What happened was, I was playing a C Melody saxophone, which I had bought, and I bought this because that was what I understood Frankie Trumbauer played, and then Willie told me -- Willie "The Lion," that is, said if I was going to play with orchestras, I'd have to have an Alto or a Tenor, because they weren't using C Melodies; you know -- there wasn't any music being written for them in the orchestral parts -- and he was quite right, at that time.

So I got an Alto saxophone, and I'll tell you a very funny thing he used to do to me, which wasn't funny, really; it was very good for me -- but in playing the C Melody saxophone, you are also always playing in the concert key, just

as the piano -- he's playing an E flat, and you're playing an E flat; he's playing in C and you're playing in C. But when I got the Alto, well, I started playing in keys or having to play in keys with which I was not familiar. The only sharp key I played in before was the one sharp which was G, but playing with Willie The Lion Smith, when he was in G, I was in four sharps, E, when he was in C, I was in 3 sharps, A, which was extremely difficult for me.

So I would adjust the mouthpiece to change the key, you know -- pull the mouthpiece out, to change the key to make it an easier key - and he used to see me doing this, and he'd give me the dickens about it and make me, you know, play in the keys I was supposed to be in, you know, he'd say, "C'mon, kid, put that mouthpiece where it should be -- push it back in". He knew, you know, every trick that I was pulling.

And then after I finally had gotten a little better control of the keys, he would just play in any key -- you never knew what he was gonna do; he caught himself sometimes trying to trick you, you know, just for fun --and it was a very valuable musical experience for me, playing with him.
Did you -- was Fats active -- Fat Warner, active around that time? He must have been, I suppose.
Yes, Fats was active. I think at that time, he was playing the organ at the Lincoln Theatre, I think
was the name of it on 135th Street. He was very active indeed. And of course ...
But you didn't have that kind of relationship with him that you had with Willie the Lion, though?
Unfortunately, I did not. No.
We'll get to your relationship with him about 20 years later.
All right.

Okay. Now, at the age of 15 or 16, you have your first paying job and presumably, you're getting known a bit around the clubs and among musicians, especially, and maybe even club owners; people who hired musicians. Was it around this time that you would say that you would begin to be a genuinely professional musician?

Well, it depends upon how you would define genuinely ... certainly it is not synonymous with complete. But you know, I was learning. I was still, of course, undergoing the learning process, which even at this point, I still am -- but that was pretty early.
Well, you know, people often say on the basis of your recordings, that one of your earliest bands that you played with was Charlie Johnsons.
Yes.
Now that didn't begin until 1927.
Here we are talking about 1922, roughly, and you've got about 5 years here. Can you roughly fill in a little bit?
Well, maybe actually ...
Can you do a little memory jogging of what went on at that time?

Good. Maybe what I'm talking about is really, probably, a little later than '22, because I know that I did play with Billy Fowler, who else did I play with? I did some playing around New York with, oh, some bands who did -- Charlie Matson.
Was that MATSON?
M-a-t-s-o-n. Right. Gee whiz, who else?
I think Billy Page?
Well, Billy Page ... now, in ...
Did that come later?
Well, that came probably later. Because in 1925,, and let me get my -- let me jog my memory, if I can.
Certainly.

In 1925, there was a band that came to New York called the Broadway Syncopators -- that was Billy Page -- and they played at a place called the Capitol -- it was Capitol something, but it was a big cabaret in New York, a nightclub, and I think they had a saxophone player
with them named Vance Dixon, who had a fine reputation -- a very, very fine clarinetist and saxophonist. And he left and I was hard to replace the band there -- I replaced the Alto player.
And following that engagement, he asked me if I would go to Pittsburgh with them. They were from Pittsburgh; that was their home base.
Uh huh.

So I ... in 1925, I guess I was almost 18? Yes. That's right. So, I went to Pittsburgh with them and for one reason I wanted to go, I had, you know, part of my family in a place called Macdonald, Pennsylvania, where I had gone to school for a short while earlier, and where my cousin, Cuban Bennett lived.

So I went to Pittsburgh with Billy Page's orchestra. I worked with him there a short while. And then I went to work with Earl Hines -- with the sextet that Earl Hines had, and I think I played baritone saxophone with the sextet.
And that was all in Pittsburgh?
That was all in Pittsburgh.
Uh huh.
And then a band came through there, Horace Henderson and His Collegians -- during my time, oh, this must have been 1926, I guess.
So you must've stayed in Pittsburgh for a while?
Yes, I did stay in Pittsburgh for a while.
You had gone there at 18, and let's say in 1925, about, somewhere in there -- you played with Billy Page, you played with Earl Hines for awhile.
Right.
And then you say somewhere -- maybe in 1926 -- you ...

Yes. Well, actually, I played for a very short while with Roy Eldridge and his brother, Joe. They had an orchestra called the Elite Serenaders or Elite Syncopators, I don't know ... probably the Elite Serenaders.
And that was also in Pittsburgh?
That was also in Pittsburgh.
Uh huh. Then Horace Henderson comes through with the Collegians.
With the Collegians.
Right. Do you remember the circumstances of your going with them?
I know that there had been -- I'm trying to think -- I think I played a couple of gigs around there with them. Was it in Pittsburgh, or around Pittsburgh? In the area, though. Following which, he
asked me if I would, you know, like to join the band. And I thought it over; well, I would just say that finally, I agreed to go, you know, and I went to work with them.
Uh huh. Now, did they play regularly in Wilburforce, or did they take dates out of Wilburforce?
Yes, they took dates going out of Wilburforce quite often. That's right. They were located there.
But they were not really playing on a campus all the time.
Sometimes. Not all the time, oh, certainly not.
But that wasn't why they stayed there.
No, that wasn't. No.
So that brings us to about '26 or '27.
Yes.
Right?
Uh huh.
And did you ever go on the road with Horace Henderson and the Collegians?
Oh yes, yes. We went on the road. And then finally, we were getting some arrangements from Fletcher, his brother, Fletcher Henderson -- and then I
think that Fletcher arranged an engagement for the band in a place called the Club Bamville. I think, which was at 129th Street and Lenox Avenue at the time.
Was it B-A-M?
That must come from 'Alabama', I think, right?
I would think so. Yes. I think so.
Okay. So ...

I'm thinking ... some of the musicians were going to graduate at the end of that particular semester, and those who weren't elected to just not go back to school to keep the orchestra together. You know, they opted for the music rather than whatever else they were majoring in, I don't know.

But ... I'm trying to think what happened with Charlie Johnson, because I went with Charlie Johnson, it seems and then I wound up again with the Henderson band -- with Horace Henderson again. Or, did I ... I'm trying to figure, because if I was with Charlie Johnson in 1927...
Yes. Well, I think that you went with -- you must have gone back with Horace Henderson a bit later.
Yes.
Because maybe when you played the
Club Bamville, with Horace Henderson, and then you went on to Charlie Johnson, because that must have been around 1927. Then you played with Charlie Johnson and that was at the Paradise Club.
That was at ... yes, Small's Paradise.
Small's Paradise, yes. Then you made some recordings with Charlie Johnson.
That's right.
Then I think you went back again and they toured with Horace Henderson, and then you got to Detroit, I remember, or I believe, if I remember read correctly.
Yes, that's correct.
And then in 1928, that was the time of the award that was made to that band.
That ... what was it -- did it say the King of Jazz or was it ...
Right. The Jazz King of America.
The Jazz King of America; yes, that was in a battle of music at the Greystone Ballroom, with McKinney's the McKinney Cottonpickers.
Right.
And I still have that trophy on that big gold plated cup or lacquered -- whatever it is, which rightfully, belongs to Horace, because Horace was the leader
of the band at that time, but when Horace left the band, I don't even remember how it happened to come in to my possession, but ...
But you took over that band, though, when he found it necessary to leave.
That's right. I was elected the leader.
Right. It was the summer of 1928 and he had to go -- he had some personal business. The band then asked you to take over.
That's correct.

And then the award was made to the band, but you, as the leader, took it --and I have a note about it -- it says, 'Jazz Award Cup presented as first prize to the Jazz King of America at the Greystone Garden August 13, 1928 in Detroit, Michigan.'
That's it.
I once took that off the plaque that you once showed me in your living room.
Oh yes, yes. Well, that's it.

Now, we're down to ... let's call a halt here for a moment. You are now 20 years old, 21 -- pretty well known as a musician; you played with Earl Hines, Billy Fowler, Billy Page, Charlie Johnson, Horace Henderson -- and you're about, I think, to join Fletcher Henderson, somewhere in here.
Somewhere in there.
Right. Okay. Now, let's go on to the subject of arranging.
Yes.
Now when did the arranging come in, and let's bring that up to 1928, sort of, or up to the point where you joined Fletcher Henderson.

Actually, I started arranging when I was with Charlie Johnson's orchestra at the Small's Paradise. I started arranging by writing saxophone choruses, you know, for 3 saxophones, because that's what we had then, and there were 3 saxophones -- Benny Whittet, Benny Waters and Benny Carter. Three Bennys in the saxophone section.

And I used to write the saxophone choruses, you know, the rhythm section, because they knew all the chord changes and I knew the chord changes, but I didn't know how to do anything else. And I decided I wanted to arrange. I started studying what they called 'stock arrangements' -- arrangements by Don Redman, Archie Blyer, Arthur Lang, Walter Paul; I guess, Jimmy Dale, Jack Mason ... these are the names I remember, and I used to layout the parts on the floor and study them. And I started arranging just like that; part by part -- starting with the first trumpet, second trumpet, etc., and was oh, I guess, quite -- it was quite a matter of months before I knew how to make a score, you know? Because
I was doing it the hard way.
Yeah. Let me go back for a moment. You started the actual arranging, and your arrangements were used when you were with Charlie Johnson, let's say, 1927?
Yes.
But had you been interested in arranging? Did you have some ambition to arrange? Had you made some attempts on your own which were not arrangements that perhaps were not actually used?
Well, I don't remember that I did. I don't think I did anything for the Henderson band, you know, Horace Henderson, that is.
Did Charlie Johnson ask you to do some arrangements, or did you ...

No, I just started bringing these things and I would ask other saxophone players to join me and try them, you know ... like if we'd play a song like "I Got Rhythm" or one of the, you know, we'd use the saxophone chorus in the arrangement or something. Even if it was somebody else's arrangement or something.
I see. And the musicians liked them, or at least the musicians liked them.
Yes, they seemed to like them.
And when you say you learned the hard way, you didn't have a teacher, also? Nobody said to
No, I didn't have enough sense to do that. That was too easy.
Yeah, always the hard way.

Always the hard way. Just like with the trumpet. You know, I took it home and I thought I was gonna be an instant Cuban Bennett, you know, and then another name that I got to throw in here -- maybe it might be a little early -- but was a man whom I hadn't been influenced greatly yet, but was Doc Cheatham.
Uh huh. On trumpet.
Oh yes indeed.
All right. Let's go to the trumpet. Now when did you begin to go back to the trumpet? You had dropped it for the alto. When did you start returning to the trumpet?
Well, about 1929, I had an orchestra at the Arcadia Ballroom, I believe that was at 53rd Street and Broadway.
Right.

And in that trumpet section was Doc Cheatham, and I absolutely loved his playing and his sound, and he knew that I was interested in trumpet, and I was really afraid to tackle the trumpet at that point, because I was afraid it would interfere with my saxophone career. He

assured me that it wouldn't. He said that he had also played saxophone before, and I believe it hadn't bothered him, but he didn't continue to play saxophone because it was hard devoting time to both instruments.

And he encouraged me, and I didn't have an instrument, and he used to reach over to the saxophones from back in the trumpet section and give me his trumpet and tell me to go on up to the mike and play a solo, you know, which I ...
And had the temerity to do?
Oh yes. I had a lot of chutzpah, you know. But with his encouragement, I really decided that I would get a trumpet and really practice it, which I did, eventually --and he helped me a great deal.
Uh huh. Did you like his style? Were you attracted to his style, or was it his tone or both?
Oh, it was all of it. His style, his sound that he got, the ease with which he did everything he did. Yes, oh yes.
And of course he is still playing that trumpet.
Yes, he is.
We just heard him this past weekend. In New Jersey.
I played with his niece last year, and ...
Then they made a recording with him for Jeff Muldaur, a vocalist, and we had a large band,
and Doc was in there, too.
That's right. And I just played with him up at Monterey -- the Monterey Festival.
Oh yes.
We did a tribute to ...
Fletcher?
No. Well, yes, a tribute to Fletcher, but we did a tribute to Louis Armstrong, and 6 trumpet players, each of whom played a chorus.
Really? I didn't know that.

Yes, he played a chorus, I played a chorus on trumpet, Clark Terry, Claude Perry, Dizzy Gillespie, John Faddis, and ... is that 6? Dizzy Gillespie, Claude Perry, Clark Terry, Doc Cheatham, Faddis, Carter -- Faddis, Carter -- who was the other one? There was another one -- there were 6 of us. Harry Edison.
Harry Edison.
Oh, how I could forget him! Sweets?
That's six. Okay, so you came to the trumpet then, again, around '28 or '29 -- but that was '29 when you had your own band.

That was '29 when I had my own band for a short period, and my cousin, Cuban Bennett, had been in New York for quite a while, and I, you know, got to hear more of him than I had been hearing. Unfortunately, he never did record. Someone told me that he had made records, but I
never heard any of them.
I've never heard of any. I've heard of people who know about him ...
Yes.
But I don't know; I've never heard of any actual records. That he may have made.
No. Nor have I.

I'd like to come now, you know -- we brought up your sax playing, your arranging, and your interest in the trumpet and your taking up the trumpet, which brings us to somewhere in 1928-29. Now let's go on to the band-leading and playing and other things that came up after that point. I'd like to get some notion -- is the next major thing that you do going to Fletcher Henderson's band, or is there something else that goes on before that?
Let me see ... I'm trying to remember when if I was with Chick Webb's band.
I think that came later.
I was with Fletcher first and then Chick's, and then did I go back to Fletcher, I think?
I think so. Yes. I think you went in and out.
Yeah, that's what I thought happened.
Do you remember your first entry into Fletcher's band -- do you remember how that happened?
Yes.
I think it had something to do with Don Redman?
Yes. I was playing with Billy Fowler at a club called the Cameo Club.
Uh huh. In Harlem or was that downtown?
It was in New York ... oh no, downtown.
Downtown, uh huh.

And Fletcher was playing at Roseland. Don Redman -- if I'm correct about this -- I think that Don Redman's father, or someone in the family passed, and Don had to go to Piedmont,West Virginia, which I think was his hometown, and he was going to be gone a week or two, and Fletcher asked me if I could come in and sub for him during that period. This was a great opportunity for me, I felt, because if you were asked to play with Fletcher, I kind of felt that this was reserved for the guys who were considered really tops in whatever they were doing, and I spoke to Billy Fowler about it, feeling maybe he wouldn't let me off to do it -- and he encouraged me to do it. He was very considerate. He knew it meant a lot to me to play with Fletcher Henderson, and he encouraged me to do it.
I went and played with Henderson for that period, and that was just a great, great thing for me.
You went in and out of Fletcher's band.
Yes.
Around that time?
Yes, I did, because then when Don finally went with McKinney's Cottonpickers, Fletcher invited me in to the band to replace Don.
Uh huh. And then of course, you had already been with McKinney's Cottonpickers before that.
No. No, I was never with McKinney's Cottonpickers before Don was.
That's right.
No, but I had recorded with them.
You had recorded with them when Horace -- wasn't that the Horace period?

I recorded with them when Don -- what used to happen, if I remember correctly, is that you know, they were a great touring band; they did a lot of road work, and Don used to come in town to record, I believe, under the McKinney's Cottonpickers name, and -- or maybe it was under the name of the Chocolate Dandys, but anyway -- he would put a band together, you know. I believe Gene Coleman Hawkins, myself, Fats Waller on piano.
Yeah.
But I didn't play with McKinney's Cottonpickers until I was again asked to replace Don.
I see.
You see? Yeah, so I replaced Don with Fletcher, and then replaced him again with McKinney.

Uh huh. In your own arranging, did you work closely in any way, or did you go to Don Redman for advice -- how did your arranging at that time ... you arranged for Fletcher Henderson -- he did, I guess.
Oh, yes. He did.
Chocolate Dandies?
You arranged for the trumpet.
Yes.
You arranged for McKinney's Cotton-Pickers, and he did.
Yes.
Were all these things coincidences, or was there some designed connection between your work in arranging and his?
Well, strangely enough, I think it was all coincidental.
All coincidental.
Yeah. I really do think so.
Right. Well, then it was in there that you became associated with -- you went to Chick Webb's around the early 30's, I think.
Yes, that's right. '31.
'31. Right.
Yes.

Right. Now you had already had a band for a short time. When did you -- I think ... now let's go to composing. And let's try to remember where we are; we are somewhere around 1931 where you -- after this experience with a few bands, you are now with Chick Webb, again, for a short time. With composing, when did you begin to compose? Do you remember?
Well, the first song I wrote was a song ... well, I wrote a number of songs in the early days, but the first one that was published was "Blues in My Heart" and that was in 1931.
Were you at that time -- do you remember being with Chick Webb at that time?
No. At that time, I was with Fletcher Henderson. We were playing at Connie's Carney's Inn.
Right. And was that written, in a sense, for the Henderson band?
No.
You just wrote it ...
I just wrote it ... just a song I wrote, you know?
