Oh yes. Yes.
Right. But that was not the Connie's Carney's Inn and so on, which was for whites and which discouraged blacks from coming in.
That's right. Connie's Carney's Inn, and the Cotton Club, they really did not welcome the black customer.
Uh huh. Now maybe this is as good a place as any to talk about questions of race.
Uh huh.
And discrimination and the role of the black musician. Now you played places ... I don't mean, you personally, but the musician would play downtown and uptown -- uptown meaning Harlem.
Harlem, yes.
Were the conditions different in the two places? Pay better downtown or anything, or was it all the same?

I guess downtown would pay better. The situation there was that, oh, I'm trying to remember ... yes, the downtown pay, I believe was better. It's even hard for me to remember what kind of money we ... as long as -- what I want to say is -- according to the AFM -- the American

Federation of Musicians -- scale, they would have a higher scale downtown, you know, like maybe a place like the Roseland would be a Class A and someplace else would be a Class B, and maybe the Harlem clubs would be a Class B and a Class C, you know. I don't know if there were any Harlem clubs that they considered Class A.
I kind of doubt it. But if they did, they would probably be places like the Cotton Club where or the Ellington or the Calloway orchestra usually played.

Before we go on again to this question of discrimination, another thought occurs to me. Here you are playing in the early 20's, mid 20's, late 20's -- and we're down again now in the early 30's, and all this is New York music; you'd been to Pittsburgh -- Teddy Wilson came from Chicago, what about New Orleans? Do you hear anything about New Orleans at that time? Is New Orleans something known in New York as a particular kind of music, or is New York its own little hotbed and source of music?

Yes and no. New Orleans was certainly known, and the music was very popular; as a matter of fact, Louis Louis Russell came with an orchestra that included Paul Barbarin on drums and Henry 'Red' Allen, both you know, all great New Orleans players. And they raised a pretty good stir in New York, and Jelly Roll General Morton came to New York, if I believe -- he was a New Orleans player, wasn't he?
Of course, sure.
And who else from New orleans? Of course when Barney Bagard joined Ellington, I think Braud was from New Orleans -- Wellman Braud Brew?
Yes.
The bassist. And New Orleans musicians were known and highly respected.
In New York?
Oh yes. Yes indeed.
Uh huh. Was it a particular style, or just you knew that there were people from New Orleans?
Oh no. It was a style, of course.
It was a style.
Yes.
Did New York players coniciously try to play New Orleans, some of them?
No doubt they did. I couldn't site any particular examples, you know, but ...
Was it a kind of music, let's say, that was as sharply marked in the 20's as you recall it, as let's say, bop was in the early 40's?
I don't think so.
No.
No. It didn't have that kind of impact.
It mingled much more with what everybody was doing.
Yes. It wasn't as innovative.
And if there had been no players coming from New Orleans, New York music would have gone on the way it did, more or less the same?
Yes, I think so. Yes, I think it would be quite safe to say that.

Because this is an interesting thing about trying to recapture what the meaning of New Orleans was in other places. It seemed to have had a much greater impact in Chicago, perhaps, than it did in New York. But who knows?
Yeah.
I mean it's interesting.

Well, I don't know. The interesting thing about New York jazz, though, was look at the pianists that came from New York -- Fats Waller, J.P. Johnson, Willie 'the Lion' Smith, you know, from Newark, originally, but he really came up in New York, I think.
Oh sure. Sure.
And this was really the center for the pianists.
Yeah. Well, a lot of times in jazz history, certain conceptions arise because they are early conceptions, and they go on and on and people don't
think of examining these older ideas. I'm not making any claim about the relative influence of New Orleans as against another place, but I think it's something worth discussing, as we have been.
Yeah, sure.

Let me go back to the question of race relations and discrimination. Did you have a sense that there was at that time, that there was another world of music which the black musician was not able to penetrate?
Oh yes.
Uh huh.
What world was that? What sort of recollections do you have about that?
Well, that was downtown.
Downtown.
That was downtown and of course, in addition to the clubs and the shows, the pit bands in the shows, you know, there was radio.
Right.
And there were no black musicians in radio at all.
Are you talking now even about the mid and late 1920's?
Oh yes.
Before the 30's begin? Before
swing, I mean?
Yes, because the staff orchestras were ...
Ah, yes.
You know, they were ... I mean, they were just staff orchestras -- the guys who were making $400 and $500 a week. You know, and we were up at the Savoy making $33, you know?
You knew those things were there, and that they were closed to you?
Oh, of course. Oh yes.
And you knew the music?
Oh yes.
Well, what sort of attitude did you have towards the music itself? Let's hear just for a moment about that.
How did you mean 'attitude toward the music'?
Well, did you think it was good music, bad music, or whatever it was -- was it music that you could do?
Oh, certainly it was good music. Yes, But I mean, of course, we always felt that there were musicians who could do it just as well.
Right.

But the opportunity was denied them. In addition to the fact that in Harlem, many white musicians used to come in and listen to the black musicians, and not only listen, but sit in with them. Quite often. But we couldn't go downtown and sit in with them.
Did blacks ...
Or even listen to them, you know?
Right. Did black musicians feel that white musicians would come in and pick up things which they could then use in their own way also? Was that part of it?
Oh, yes, of course. I mean, of course, they could pick up things from records, as far as that went.
Yes. They didn't have to ...

Yes, they didn't have to come and play and sit in with us, you know, but I think that helped, and I think our exposure to them helped us, too, you know. I think it was, you know, a matter of a change.

Right. And nobody, of course, in those days -- let's talk still about up to 1933 or so, because that's a kind of -- when you formed your band is the period we're stopping at and we're gonna take up after that.
Okay.
Up until say, about 1933, the end of 1933, white and black musicians did not play together on
regular dates. They could play together in Harlem, after hours, or even during hours, but not downtown during hours, and not on formal regular dates.
Not that I was aware of.
Right. You don't remember anything of that sort going on?
No, no.
Blacks, of course, felt -- knew and realized that a whole world of musical opportunities was denied them.
They felt it was definitely closed to them, you know.

And was there any sense that -- well, I guess then also, if whites came in and sat in with musicians in Harlem, there must have been some sense that the -- musically, this was a ridiculous situation, because the guys were enjoying playing together.
Oh, yes indeed. Sure. We'd welcome them. Certainly. We enjoyed it.
Uh huh. Did some of the black musicians, in your recollection, feel that maybe these white musicians could have tried a little bit harder to open up some opportunities for black musicians?
Well, I don't know. I don't remember, you know, harboring that feeling or noting it in anyone else.
Maybe we just kind of at that moment at been sort of resigned ourselves to the situation as it was and feeling maybe that even the white musicians themselves couldn't do anything about it, you know?
Uh huh. That it was the whole social situation ...
Yes.
And segregation and bookings and so on.
Right. The whole system.

Yeah. Well, that brings us now to the -- let me go back now to your band. I don't think that we talked about the impulses that led you to the formation of this band in 1932 when it was a rehearsal band and you made some records, and then you found some dates -- do you remember particularly when this band, in a sense, took off? You know, when did you begin to have regular employment, jobs, and you had a group which was identifiable as the Benny Carter Band or Orchestra, without too many changes in personnel?

Oh, that ... I don't think that ever really happened. I mean, no, not really. There's always been a lot of changes in personnel because all of the bands that I've ever had never stayed together too long, even at that period, I think, we went in to the Savoy Ball-

room in 1933 for a short period, and gee, I don't remember at the moment how long that band lasted, but you know, I was doing arrangements for different bands around town and I guess every time there would be a lean period when the band had no work, I would start doing some writing for somebody.
Right.

And I think that would even leave the members of the band to think that I didn't have a great motivation for keeping the band together because if the band didn't stay together, even if they couldn't eat, I could. You know? And I could understand their feelings very well, and of course, in retrospect, I can understand it much better now than even then, you know?
Yeah.
But I think if I hadn't been able to write, I might have done more with the band; I would have been more motivated to keep it together.
Sort of enforced or something?
Yeah. Right. Absolutely. That's what I really feel. You know.
Yeah. Well, you know, historians of jazz, and people who have written about you have said that your bands were always critical and artistic successes, but not commercial successes.
Yes.

What you're saying then, is that if you had been forced by some necessity to work with these bands and to make them commercial successes, who know? Maybe they might have become -- their chances might have been improved.
Right.
But, at the moment, of course, it's always difficult at the time when it happens to say, well, I won't eat. Let's keep the band together.
Right.
How could you do that?
Right. That's true.
You couldn't keep a band together if you didn't eat.
That's right ... very true.
This band -- did you have some particular motive and style of music that you wanted to get played with this band that forms in '32 and '33 and which Teddy Wilson joins?

No. I don't think I did, and I think that had another thing, maybe - had something else to do with the band not becoming a great commercial success. I don't think any band I ever had had a really identifiable Benny Carter sound. You know, like ... I think the Goodman band developed that and of course, the Glenn Miller Band,
which was not really a swing or a jazz band. They had that by virtue of the sound of the clarinet lead thing and certain other things. But I don't know; maybe ...

Of course, it was not until about '34 or '35, wasn't it -- that all these bands kept coming up with rippling rhythm and all these things, because there were so many of them that they had to have something ...
An identity.
Something to identify them with.
Identity, yes.
But in the early 30's or late 20's -- let's say, did Duke have some gimmick like that? I don't remember any.
Well, I think Duke has always had a sound, but without a gimmick, you know?
Yes. Well, I think a lot of people would say that your bands have always had a sound.
Really?
Oh, I think so. But again, without a gimmick.
Yes.

I mean it was not something like that, and it seems that for a popular success though, which is what we're talking about now, it seems you have to have some identifiable quality. People like to be able to recognize
things.
The next tape with Benny Carter. We've been discussing differences in the bands and the kinds of distinctive gimmick sounds they seem to require in the early Swing era.

So I was saying, briefly, that they liked to have these distinctive sounds which the fans could recognize, but the fans also liked to have the bands do the same things all the time so they could feel comfortable and secure with that too.
Now in this competition among these bands, something that got called 'swing' developed, let's say, somewhere in the early 30's. When do you -- do you remember the use of that word at all?

I think that word came in to -- well, not the word, but the term as applied, you know, to the type of music -- came in to wide usage just, oh, I believe, during my stay in Europe. I don't know ... I went to Europe in '35. When did this term start gaining momentum?

Well, I think that people may have been using it, you know, maybe musicians began using it earlier among themselves that this music swings or this guy is swinging. You remember it, of course, in that way. What did it mean at that time?
Yeah. Well, what I'm thinking of
actually, I was what they call the Swing Bands, or the King of Swing.
No, I'm not ...
Or the Swing Era or something like that.
No, that's a public relations concoction.
Madison Avenue thing.
It has a lot to do with that.
Yes.
But in the earlier usage, by musicians among themselves, the word 'swing' was frequently used, wasn't it?

Yes, it was. As a matter of fact, I even remember now that when I went to Paris in 1935, I had a conversation about that with Hugues Panassie. And I think he used some French term for 'swing' that I think was -- my French is pretty bad at this point, but it seems it was Espes de la Banceloin. (PHONETIC)
Oh really?
Now what does that mean in French?
Was it a type of balancing?
I guess so. I don't know how to spell that word.
It was a form of it or a type of it.
A form of balance? I guess that's
it, you know. But I think that was -- not necessarily his definition of it, but you know, maybe the French counterpart of the thing or something.
Did the musicians use that, in you experience, now?
Now? Swing?
Yeah, this guy really swings.
Yes.
Or his music swings.
Oh yes. Yes.
And do they mean what they meant years ago? More or less?
I think the musicians mean what they meant years ago, yes, I think so.
Yeah. Do I take it that that is not a term that you use personally? You don't think it's very descriptive?
I guess I do, but I don't know that ...
How does this word strike you as a musical term?
I guess it's a valid term. Of course at this point, I don't even like 'jazz' as a, you know, valid term, but what -- so don't ask me for a definition of jazz, because ...
All right. But what's wrong with
'jazz' as a valid term? Why don't you like 'jazz' -- I'm not asking what it is, but why ... what connotation does it have?
All right, because I think it attempts to cover too much. It's an umbrella term that I think should not really have under it the music of Buddy Bolden and the music of Chick Corea.
Uh huh. And it does cover them both.
It does cover those. Yes. And I think that's a little too broad for one term.

Well, I'm glad that you mentioned that. Let me go back to something even before that. And we'll come back again to swing. Let's go back to the time when you were practicing as a kid and learning how to play.

Did you know that there was something called 'jazz' or were you just learning to play the music that you heard that Bubber Miley was associated with? Could it have been that you, if the opportunities had presented themselves, or if you had had the occasion to think of it, that you might have become a symphony player or something. Did you have goals specifically directed towards jazz music as something called 'jazz'?
Well, I guess I did, because I suppose that, as a black or a Negro, as I termed myself at that time,

I felt that there was no future in being a symphonic musician. I didn't know of any black musicians playing with symphony orchestras, and I knew even very few string players; just a couple of violinists, and those that I knew played jazz. You know, or what they called jazz.
Did you have some idea, however, of going beyond what was known as jazz or the music that blacks or Negros were playing at that time?
At that very early period, no. I think I just wanted to play and I didn't take into consideration very much the future that I was headed for.
When did you begin to be dissatisfied with jazz as a term either for what you were doing or what everybody was doing?
Oh, fairly recently. When I say fairly recently, at my age, fairly recently can be any time within the last 20 years, you know? So probably about 20 years ago.
And does that have something to do also with your composing? Your writing music?
Not necessarily. I think that it has more to do with the different types of music and the realization of jazz, so called, is really a basically Afro-American music. You know?
Yes.
Because we have the old argument,

which goes do you really think there are no whites who can play jazz? Well, I don't know whether whites can play jazz or not. I know there are whites who play a lot of music that I like. Now, if somebody wants to call it jazz, you know, fine. There are blacks that play a lot of music I like. If somebody wants to call it jazz, fine.
Right.
But you know, I think that young black musicians have gone back to the roots, more recently than in my early days they were doing.
Right.

Now when they became very conious of being black and filled with this Black Pride and went back to really get at the roots of jazz or at the roots of black music, the music that I've heard since then is much more what maybe they meant by the term 'jazz' in the old days. When the term first came into being.

Would you say it represents something like this -- that when you came up and were growing up and were learning your instruments and arranging and so on, there was no question, as you mentioned earlier, that you did aspire to do what blacks were doing, because there were no other opportunities.
Right.
So you did it, and what you wanted to do was to be as proficient as you could be at
it and to -- and not to worry where it came from or what it was, because it was all around you. You didn't have to think about that.
Right.
But nowadays, with the intervening years and greater opportunities and more schooling of black musicians, they have a greater choice. They can do one thing, or they can choose to do another.
They have more choice. They have a greater consciousness of the origins of their music than I had; than I even allowed myself to think about.
Right. So that they want to go back to that because that is now available to them in a way that it didn't need to be available to you because it was all that was around you.
Right.

There was no question of choice. Now these guys can play for symphonies, they can arrange for different ways, so they have to -- they go back consciously to the jazz roots, whereas you were, in a sense, trying to get anywhere that you could go where your music would take you.
That's right. Absolutely.
Right.
That's it.
That's very funny, because I
think this is a phenomenon that happens to a lot of other domains of life.
Indeed.
Where you get a choice and -- which other people didn't have and then the choice goes back to the thing that the people who grew up with it didn't know it was a choice; that's all they knew.
Yes, yes, yes.
That was all that was available to them. Okay. Do you want to add something to this? I'm sorry ...

Well, I have no specific question, but I wanted to go back to the Swing idea. Swing, now, not as a term, describing a particular kind of music, in the technical sense, but Swing as the kind of social musical phenomenon in this country.

The Swing Era people say it begins in 1933, '34, '35 -- you know, you can pick different events. Some people say that it begins with Benny Goodman, when he was on the road during 1934, he played in New York. Of course, you were still here. In fact, you were arranging for him, I believe, at the time you went in to Billy Rose's Music Hall.
The Music Hall.
Right. Then he got on the "Let's Dance" program. When that ended, he began to tour. When he began to tour, that's when you toured in the other
Right.
He wound up in -- he made a tremendous hit with some Fletcher Henderson arrangements, it seems, as people recall it, in the Palamar Ballroom, was it? Or something in Los Angeles?
I guess so.

Right. And he still didn't have it made, you know. Studies of his career and his bands show that he still had some way to go after that, but that stresses the big phenomenon, of all the kids loving this dance music and so on.

Now what went in to that music? You were still here at that time. When you arranged for Benny Goodman in the summer, I think it was, or the Fall of 1934, do you remember that? It was around the time you went to the Music Hall. What sort of things, if you can reconstruct that, were you arranging for him? The same sorts of things you would do for your own band, which you, I think, no longer had?
Right. I no longer had the band. When I arranged for Goodman ... gee ... I did mostly pop tunes, you know, like 'It Happens to the Best of Friends' and 'I'm a Builder Upper', and ...
Yeah. But these are not songs, let's
No. Probably not songs that at that time I would have arranged for myself, although I did in later years, you know, like in about 1939 at the Savoy, I did some kind of junk junk tunes for myself.
What did you call them?
Junk tunes.
Junk tunes, yeah.
Yeah. Some of them weren't particularly outstanding.
Would you call them 'pop' tunes?
Yeah, pop tunes.
You mean commercial, Tin Pan Alley things?
Commercial, Tin Pan Alley tunes, that's right. Yeah.
And what sort of arrangements would you have called them at that time? Let's say that you were making ...
Well, I'd say in the vernacular of the day they would have been swing arrangements.
Uh huh. You arranged for Benny Goodman before between Fletcher Henderson did -- did you know that?
Yes. Yes, I did know that.
You remember that?
As a matter of fact, his first recording session which I think was August 16th or something -- or 14th, 1934. Am I right? In 1934, he recorded my arrangement of "Lonesome Nights".
Right.
And I think they say that was his first recording or something, I don't know.
Well, he had recorded, I think, with bands under other -- led by other people.
Yes.
I think that may have been his first Benny Goodman orchestra as it became known.
That's what I mean. Yes.
Yes, at that time. What were you hearing? I mean you went to Europe in I think April or May of '35.
Yes.
What were you hearing in Europe about what was going on in the States? About music? Do you remember anything about that?

Let me see ... what was I hearing? I guess I was ... like, I can't remember, no. No. I don't remember. I know that with the people like Charles Delauney, DeLome, you know, who did what I remember as being the first discography, maybe there was one before him; I don't know. And oh, Hugh Pannassie Le Jazz Hot. Hugues Benasier, who had written a book, I think,
Right.
They were all, you know, caught up in the interest of American music. And ... gee, I don't remember what they were saying about it.
You don't have any recollection today about what you might have been thinking about?
No. I don't.
And so far as you know or recall, what did Benny Goodman and these other groups like groups led by T. Teagarden or Ben Pollack, you knew about those groups?
Oh, sure.

Did you regard them as playing the kind of music that you played -- the kind of things that Fletcher Henderson was involved in? Chick Webb, and then when others came up in later? How did you classify it?
Somewhat. Yes. Somewhat, yes.
Uh huh.

Yes, I thought so. And of course, in Europe, you know, to talk about the term, jazz, which I guess we might as well use as a frame of reference for identification purposes, from what I felt and what even many Europeans feel today, I believe, they don't think that anybody plays jazz but the black musicians. You know?
Right.
They find it very difficult to accept

a white American as a jazz player. But I think they probably feel more strongly against thinking of him as an originator, because I know there are many white musicians who go to Europe and do very well and they are highly respected and highly thought of.

I know that when I played Nice the year before last, in 19 -- when was it, last year? 1975, it was. People like Ruby Braff and George Barnes and, oh, gee, Zoot Sims, I believe, they just loved them, you know? I'm trying to think who else was with us. A lot of breth, of our lighter-hued, you know.
I know I just did a tour this year, too, which we had Ralph Sutton, the pianist, Art Hodes, and ..
Uh huh. People don't make those distinctions.
No, they don't. No. They just loved them, you know. It's different than it used to be -- for everybody.
Better, do you think?
I think so, yes.
These musical distinctions are made by people who really don't know much about it after the fact are not at all a whole lot all that useful.
That's true.
They're useful to the people who make it, but it doesn't mean enough to musicians to be worthwhile preserving, perhaps.
Oh, I agree.
Uh huh. Do you think that it's a worthwhile enterprise to try to find out the origin and the development of Swing? That's a provocative question.
All right. Let me see what kind of an answer it can provoke me to. Provoke me to?
Sure.

All right. For me, it isn't, you know. I don't think these terms have any particular significance. If the music is good and it moves you, fine, you know. Like I had a friend who took me to hear a musician a couple weeks ago back in California that he thought was fantastic. Of course, this man was an agent, and the musician was one of his clients, and he had been asking me for quite some time to go and hear this musician with him. And I went and heard him, and after sitting through about 3 sets, when we left, you know ... before we left, I made no comment and when we left and got out in the car, he said, "Well? What did you think about so and so?" I said, "Well, he dazzled me but he didn't move me." And he had fantastic technique in what he did, you know, he was really outstanding technically, but I didn't feel that I was excited by the emotions that he, you know, stirred within me.

So I guess it has something to do with that. It either moves you or it doesn't.
The technique has to be something which is part of the man's capacity to move you?
Yes.
It isn't something that you notice apart from his great ability. If it's something that's apart from it, then it's kind of an isolated technique with not enough relation to what makes music swing.
Swing! Yes!
Or what makes people like music.
Yes. That's it.
Or at least in this case, what you like in music.
Yes, right.

So maybe it would be best if we don't pursue the discussion about the origins and the development of Swing -- because, you know, just to explain why I raised the question is this -- that people are always trying to find out, well, when did Swing begin and who should get the credit for it, and there's always a distinction that people make -- well, these guys made all the money and other people deserve all the credit and they didn't get the money and so on.
Well, we won't have that problem with jazz. About who originated it. Because Jelly Roll Morton says he invented it!
Right. He didn't give us much a month more of a date, I don't think.
No. No patent number.

Right. Well, that's why people are interested in these things, and I think that -- you know -- that many fans and many writers like to say that your true role in the development of Swing and the background of Swing -- not in Swing itself necessarily, has been underestimated, and that is somehow regarded as a compliment to you; that you played a bigger role than you've been given credit for.
Well, as a matter of fact, I've been called the "Father of Swing". They could have been even less kind -- they could have said Grandfather!
Right. But you don't reject that title, do you? That doesn't bother you.
What do you mean -- the Father of Swing?
Yes, the Father of Swing.
Yes, I do reject it because I don't think it's properly applied to the person who may have made it, you know, created Swing. I certainly didn't.
But you couldn't say who did?
No, so therefore why should I accept such a title?
Well, I think what they mean is ...
That's just like Jelly Roll Morton; I claim I invented it.
Yes. Well, you see, your fans and the writers are not so hesitant about these things. Which is appropriate.
Uh huh.

You see, this becomes a big thing; people are always looking for the first time this happened, the first time that happened, and of course, people's lives are not worked out in such a way that they always know the first time something happened, when like, I asked you, when -- what was the first recording, what was the first trumpet solo, or what did you regard yourself, or when did you pick up the trumpet again after you had put it down and so on.
Yeah.

I mean, people are interested in these things, and if you take such statments and such dates in the appropriate way, I think that they are helpful as long as you don't place too much credence in what they propose to tell.
In the answers. Well, I mean, I'm always kind of baffled by the how, when and why situation, you know?
Yes ... yeah.
'Cause I don't really know.

Well, it often leads people to make up answers, or not only to make them up, but rather, to give certain stress to things which perhaps don't deserve that degree of stress, but it becomes an answer to a question and it sounds a lot more definite, then perhaps it really was.
Sometimes it provides an answer to a question just to get rid of it.
That's it ... yes.
Right.

That happens a great deal, too, and the writers and the interviewers in jazz have only themselves to blame for the fact that very often, a response is the only way to get rid of them, and get back to the stand, where they belong, while the owner is looking on.
Right.

Okay, I think that maybe we ought to stop here and take a break, and we'll resume ... no ... one last thing I wanted to talk about before you go. I was gonna say we would resume with -- no, let's continue with two things if we can.

I want to continue. We're still with your band in 1933, and I want to continue with Spike Hughes when he comes and asks you to use your band for his recording, and then also -- what was I going to say about this other point about this period -- well, let's at least begin with Spike Hughes.
He came, I think -- was he in touch with you from England before he came here?
Well, he was, through John Hammond.
Right.

He was a friend of John Hammond's, and John had recommended to him, I believe, that he use my band. Either that, or he had asked John about my band. I don't know. But I know that John relayed to me the fact that Spike was coming and he would like to use my band, and I think he augmented it with Coleman Hawkins and Henry Red Allen, I believe, and Higginbotham -- and they were not regular members of my orchestra at the time.
And he -- you know, he's written in a very favorable way about you in one or two of his, I guess, the second of his two-volume auto-biography - I'm talking about Spike Hughes, now.
Unfortunately, I haven't yet read either one.

Oh, he said very, very nice things about you -- he said that you were the only one, you immediately understood his music and he didn't think that anybody else could see it as quickly as you saw it, and it was a great honor to have his music played by your band, which he thought was, if not the greatest, then certainly one of the greatest, and so on.

I don't ... I don't think so. I think maybe we had a rehearsal away from the studio, you know. But there wasn't a great deal. He had the music all written; everything, you know, was his arrangement and his composition, with the exception of Gabriel's Horn -- I think Someone stole "Gabriel's Horn" which I did the infamous vocal, bogo-on.
But no, everything was just done in the proper fashion.
And it was all written out?
Oh yes.
Everything.
Yes, all except of course the improvised solos like, you know ...
There were a few of those.
Oh yes, by Coleman Hawkins and Dickie Wells.
Right.

But, no, there was -- there were no hassles, no difficulties with the music. Spike was and no doubt still is, a very fine musician and it's just too bad that he didn't -- you know, there isn't more of his writing available, because I enjoyed what we did.
Did that have anything to do with your going to London later on, or was that entirely separate?
I think that was entirely separate.
Uh huh.
That was something that was brought about by Leonard Feather.
Right. Let's hold it. We'll come to that a little bit later.
Okay, we're still then; this recording with Spike Hughes is still in 1933.
Uh huh.
Do you remember how the band, how you gave up the band - did that just come out of the lack of dates, or was there a certain point at which something happened -- what is your recollection of that?
Oh, just a lack of dates, you know. We were out of the Savoy and had no place else to go.
That's the other point I wanted to ask about -- about how long did you play at the Savoy?
Probably 3 months.
And what kind of a pay scale did you have at that time?
At that time, I think the pay scale was $33 per man and $66 for leader.
Uh huh.
I think that was it. Because I'm wondering if that was in 1933 or 1939 when it was that. Maybe it was still the same in 1939, or maybe it was less in 1933. I'm not sure.
Uh huh. Did that band have any broadcasts?
Yes.
No. Not that I remember.
Broadcasts from the Savoy Ballroom came later.
In 1939 ... 1938 maybe, I don't know.
Uh huh. When did the Savoy open? Do you remember off hand?
I believe it was 1927.
Yes. And what kind of bands had they had there before? Had Chick Webb already played the Savoy by 1933, do you remember?
Well, Chick played there I think in 1931.
Earlier, I think so, yes.
You played with him then.
Yeah.
Uh huh.
But they had had, oh, they had Fess Williams.
Right.

And they had Leon Abbey. They had someone else whose name I can't remember at the moment. I can see his face before me, but I can't remember the name. MR. BERGER: Was the music you played there in this early time, early in the sense that it was in the early thirties, was that the kind of music that would be called Swing?
I suppose so, yes.
This was when the dancers were doing, what? What kind of dances were they doing?
Oh, they called it the Lindy Hop.
The Lindy Hop ... and the Big Apple? That was something else that was hot then.
Yes, The Big Apple, too. Yes.
That was not a dance between two people, that was a group, I think, dance, or something, wasn't it?
The Big Apple? No, that was a dance between 2 people. Yes.
And so at that time there were a lot of these jump junk tunes, you might call them, you know -- that people danced to.
Uh huh.
But, again, you didn't think of this
as Swing music or this kind of music or that kind of music -- you didn't think that you were now introducing something which would become known and spread all over the world as Swing music?
No. I had no idea. But we did call it Swing, you know.

Yeah. You did what you wanted. You were playing the kind of music that you wanted -- not consciously doing something that you thought that audience wanted. You were consciously trying to please an audience, dancers -- but it was in a way, in the same general direction that you yourself wanted to go and play.
Yes.
And your musicians.
Surely.
Right.
Yes.
And when the your date at the Savoy came to an end --then other regular work suddenly didn't come up?
We had some few dates, you know, casuals or out of town dates, but not, you know, of a sufficiency to warrant keeping the group together.
Right.
Well, like, you just couldn't keep
personnel together because the guys couldn't sit around waiting for you to get another job, and it was always such a hassle putting the band back together again, you know.
Yeah. These -- when the band sort of came to a grinding halt, in that period, where did most of the musicians go? Do you remember? Where did they drift off to?
To other bands or ..
Do you remember which ones?
To clubs. What? No.

Because I think there were earlier cases in which there would be movement of a considerable number of musicians from one band to another. For example, I think there was a period in there, let's say, I'd like to get your own recollection -- maybe '31 to '33 -- yeah, it would have to be '33. Let's say maybe even earlier. Let's try '29 to '33, where a lot of switching was going on between your band and Fletcher Henderson's band, including yourself.
Yes.
People would move in and out of both bands.

Well, I remember when I was with Charlie Johnson, when I left Charlie Johnson, it was to go with Fletcher Henderson, and Jimmy Harrison and I moved together from that band, from Charlie Johnson's band, in to
Henderson's band.
Right. So, one might say in a way that, well, what were the leading bands at that time?
Well, give me a year.
Let's say, when you were forming your own band in '32.
'32, '33? Well, of course, there was Ellington, there was Henderson, was there Calloway at that time?
Oh sure.
There was Calloway, there was Andy Kirk, Basie hadn't come along yet.
So there was like ...
Seems there was a Willie Lynch.
Huh?
Maybe he didn't do any recording. He had a band around; I think -- I'm a little confused about that name.

But certainly it appears to me in looking at the record that you and Fletcher Henderson had bands that were, in a sense, on a par with each other. Musicians came in and out, you played the same kind of dates and so on.
Yes.
Now I don't think that the histories, as written, would show that.
Oh? Hmm...

I think that Fletcher Henderson, who was widely regarded - and justifiably, as a very prominent and influential man, but I don't think that people realize, if you judge by the histories being written, that your band and his band were on a par in this sense that I'm talking about.

Well, I think that probably has to do with Fletcher's ability to keep his band together, you know, longer, at any given time, because of having that security of what we might call a home, quote, unquote, the Roseland Ballroom, you know? As I think of it now, I don't know of any other black band that competed with him for that job at the Roseland.
But the Savoy Ballroom, you know ...
It didn't compare in security or in pay scale.
That's right, you see.
What do you think Roseland was paying at that time?
If I remember correctly ...
Or what Fletcher was paid?
If I remember correctly, I was making $110 a week.
Uh huh.

Which was a pretty good salary. For a side man, you know, in New York. And that was probably when -- now what the scale was, I don't know. I was probably being paid over scale, but -- at the Savoy Ballroom, the scale there was $33.
It was still $33 and $66 for the leader?
Yeah, that's right. But when I worked with Fletcher, I was paid $110 a week.

Right. You know, as you indicate, this history is so fluid that, you know, you can make almost any kind of case where there is a little bit of evidence, or where there is more evidence, you can re-establish a case for a different kind of position than has been accepted for a long time. And I think that certainly, as in fact, come to think of it, Walter Allen Ella, who chronicled Fletcher Henderson so extraordinarily in that great discography and biography, has said that a lot of the things that went on at that time were not so well understood, and would repay investigation from a different point of view.

For example, with respect to your own role and the place of your arrangements and the influence that they may have had on others as against the arrangements that Fletcher Henderson did. And what were the sources of these influences. But of course, that's difficult to talk
about now, so many years later, People's memories are not easily jogged to recall all those things.
Well, maybe there would be some point to doing that. But that doesn't bother you, huh? Does it interest you very much? Establishing these things?

Well, no, because I don't see how they can be firmly established, like, you know, as you say, people's memories have to be jogged. I must admit that on some of these areas, my memory is very dim, you know? I just don't remember. And I don't mean, not necessarily going back 40 years ago, but even going back 20 years ago, you know, I can't always think of just the real firm details.

As soon as something becomes firmed in an article or a book, of course, it takes on a very hard character that is not easy to change. It spreads around a lot and -- I don't know that it's terribly earth-shaking, but you know, in the history of jazz, which has become something much more important that it used to be, it has a certain importance.
Yes, I suppose it has.
From that point of view, cultural history, and ...
Yes, yes.
It is warranted to talk about it.
Not that it would get you any closer to something up there called the truth, whatever that is, but at least it's something that people like to talk about.
But some musicians also talk about it, and others -- like yourself -- don't.
I wonder why that is!
Is it something that musicians talk about with each other? Or at least in your experience?
No, not in my experience, really.
You mean about the origins of ...
Yeah, who started what ...

No -- no, I haven't been engaged in many of these kinds of conversations. No, not seriously. I guess I'm not around musicians who were my contemporaries at the time, you know -- or enough of them that we shared the same memories of the same period.

Yeah. That's true -- but there are musicians who are often quoted on these matters, and it may be that they're quoted because somebody -- an interviewer like me presses them for something, and then we go back to the previous situation where they want to give an answer, and it's only natural for a man, if he's gonna give an answer, and a quick one, to get rid of the question, he will give an answer which puts himself perhaps in a better light, because maybe when the question is predicated upon that idea.
Are you suggesting that we can get rid of this if I say I invented Swing?
Yes. I must confess! Well, you see, I want to be the man who is forced to have made you to confess that you invented Swing.
Force me to confess!
Yes.
I did it! I did it!
You didn't mean to.
I didn't mean to, but I did it!
Yeah.

Well, I think that that establishes firmly your attitude towards this whole question. I must confess that, although I am interested in jazz history, that I think that is a very healthy attitude and it's predicated on very good grounds. You know, because there is so little that can be firmly established in this way.
Okay, I think that we will call a halt for the moment and we'll begin next time, I think, with the time that you go to Europe in the Spring of 1935 and the circumstances surrounding that decision.

Benny, I want to continue with our discussion, and I'm still not gonna get to your trip to Europe for the moment. I want to go on to one or two things which are still back in 1932. There's a little incident --

amusing perhaps -- which seems to have taken place in December of 1932 in which Fletcher Henderson used your band and a date in Pennsylvania, I believe. Do you recall that, or shall I recall it for you?
You might be able to recall it to me. I know that it was in Reading, Pennsylvania, I believe, yes.

Yes, it was. Fletcher was booked in a theatre with his band in Reading, but he was also booked for a southern tour. He wanted to help the theatre owner in Reading, so he got -- he asked you to use your band. I don't think you went there.
No, I went there too.
Oh, I see. You took your band there.
Yes.
And well, according to this story in "Hendersonia" Hedosonta (PHONETIC) by Walter Allen, Fletcher led your band in Reading, and he sent another pianist to tour the south with his own band.
Oh yes, he led my band, but ...
But you played with the band.
Oh yes.
And then, while he was there -- according to Walter Allen, the producer of the Reading show told Henderson, "In all the years that I've heard your band, it never
Really?
Yeah.
Did Fletcher tell Walter Allen this?
Well, Walter Allen has it in there...
He wasn't quoting me.
No. Well, do you remember that at all? Is that fairly accurate?
Well, I don't know. I don't remember the statement having been made.
No, I don't mean the statement.
You mean the occasion?
Yes.
Oh, yes. Yes. Sure.
So that may have been one of the first -- one of the early dates of that particular band which you put together in 1932?
Yes, it was. Surely.

Another thing, around that time. There's a -- in a discussion with Bud Freeman, that was not Bud Freeman, although he was involved -- it was Mezz Mezzrow, Mezzra -- Mezzra, in his book, 'Really the BLues' mentions that you helped him with what he calls the first interracial band; everybody's got the first interracial band -- he had it in 1933.
He says in August of 1933 he signed a contract with a financial backer to support a mixed Big Band, which had Alex Hill, as the arranger, to front it. This is in Mezzrow's Mezra's book.

He said "The following agreed to join: Joe Sullivan, Bud Freeman, Floyd O'Brien, Max Kaminsky, Gene Krupa, Eddie Condon and Pee Wee Russell. We rehearsed and the future looked good and we were okay for a sustaining program on a network, but soon after, the men in the band left him to go to a rehearsal arranged by Red McKenzie for some other guy who claimed he was a politician's son ..."
Do you remember any of these details? I mean you may not have been around ...
Not really, no.

: Then he says that he stalled off the people that were leaving him and they got Benny Carter instead. To do arrangements. He says, "I was ready to quit, and as they started out for the McKenzie-Hagen rehearsals soon after, Max Kaminsky and Bud Freeman told me not to worry; that the band was no good anyway." This rival band, you see.
Then he says, " They told me we've been rehearsing some Carter -- one Carter arrangement, the first 8 bars only, and we can't even get it out yet!"
Do you recall... well, then he said something "Benny was helping Mezra with actions rather than words." Do you recall anything about that?
No, that's what I might call an interesting anecdote, but I don't remember it.
Right. Then let's put it aside.

I received a cable from Willie Lewis, who was leading a band in Paris at a club called the "Che France" and he asked me if I would like to join the band. I was having a little difficulty in New York at the time, particularly domestic difficulty, and I decided it might be a very, very good opportunity to get away from a lot of hassling for awhile and also to get to Europe, which I felt that I would be interested in seeing Paris and you know?
Right. At that time, how long did you think you might be away? I mean what was the time frame of this whole idea?

Well, in all honesty, I wasn't sure, but I guess that when I made up my mind to go, I probably had the idea of staying forever because I took my young daughter with me, who had been in custody of my wife, and I was very, very angry about this, and I wanted her with me.
I should say had been given to --
And so I suppose that I just went with the idea of staying; I didn't know when I would come back, and I didn't even think of it at that moment.
I see. So this could have been for you a permanent change. If things went well, you were
were ready at that point.
Well, at that point, yes. If someone had offered me a 20 year contract, I probably would have signed it.
And the first place then, you went to was Paris.
Right. Yes.
You joined Willie Lewis at the Che Florence France and he, of course, was an alto sax player, wasn't he?
Yes, and a clarinetist.
And clarinetist. What did you play when you joined? Did you also play alto?
I played saxophone and -- alto, as well. as well-- yes.
Uh huh. And trumpet? or ...
Yes, I did play some trumpet then, too.
Right. What were your impressions of Paris at that time? Did it live up to your expectations? Was it a great experience for you? I suppose it must have been.

Well, it was. I was tremendously impressed. I had heard so much about of Paris, and I started playing at this club, which was a late hour club; you know, you played until the last spending customer left, and that could be 5 or 6 o'clock in the morning, and maybe even later.

Django Reinhardt
Stephane Grappelli
Philippe
You know? But I did like Paris; I met John Reinhardt and Stephen Corpelli, and Alex Combelle and oh, Phil Brun and Arthur Briggs -- people like that.
I'm just trying to think.
But you didn't record anything at that point?
Well, a little later I did, with the Willie Lewis orchestra.
Yeah, the Willie Lewis orchestra did record there, that's right.
Yes, I think that was in late '35 or early '36, it must have been.
Uh huh. And through this first 6 or 8 months you were in Paris all the time.
Yes. Yes.
There were no tours yet of the continent.
No. Actually, I did no tours with Willie Lewis. We did go and play at Cannes, I believe, with oh, for a few months or weeks, but we did no tours, no concerts.
Right. Now what was the occasion then, when you left Paris for London? How did that come about?
Well, I received a letter from Leonard Feather, and wanting to know if I would be interested in coming to London to arrange for the BBC dance orchestra,
which was led by Henry Hall. And I answered to Leonard that I would be interested, and the next thing you know, I was on my way to London, and the next thing you know, I was in London.
Yeah. Then you simply left the Willie Lewis orchestra.
Yes.
You gave them notice and went to London. You were waiting then to see what the next European or British experience would then bring.
Right.
Did you know before you went to London that you would not be allowed to play regularly, according to the union rules?
Yes, I knew that, but you know, we had the feeling that maybe after some respectable period of time, that might be relaxed a little, you know.
But it never was relaxed, though.
It never was during the time I was there with -- only one occasion when they allowed me to do one concert at the Hippodrome, you know, and at this concert, I used all British musicians.
Right. That was, I think, in '37?
I think so.
And it was -- that's the one
And that's the one that was sponsored, I believe, by the Melody Makers, right?
Right. Absolutely.
Okay, let's go back. You arrived, and ...
Oh, I must say this though.
Yes?
Speaking of the restrictions about my playing, I was not allowed to play, you know, in personal appearances, but I could do recordings, which I did.
Recordings, right. As soon as you arrived then, did you record or did you begin to arrange?
Well, I began to arrange for the BBC, you know, dance orchestra.
You had not met Henry Hall before that?
No, I had not even heard of him before.
Now this was a dance band of course, and they were interested in the kinds of arrangements that you had been doing.
Obviously, they were.
So they must have known your work already quite well.
Yes.
How did you find these musicians?
Well trained, good men, and so on? Able to do good work on these arrangements?

Oh, yes ... very well trained. Very well trained, and I might say, and I hope my British musician friends won't hate me for this, but the best jazz players that I encountered at that time were Scotsmen.
Really?
Yes.
How do you account for that?

I don't know ... I have no way to account for that at all, but strangely enough, George Chisholm, a very fine trombone player, Tommy McLerda, a trumpet player; Andy McDavett, a fine clarinetist .. oh, so many.
Where did you live in London? Do you remember exactly, or more or less exactly?
Oh, I lived ... where did I live? I lived in a community called Maida Vale. Madaville.
Oh yes.
Which was not exactly suburban, but just a little way from the central city.
Right. And that's where the BBC studios were.
That's right.
So you were not very far from the recording site?
That's right. That's right.
So when you did a tune for them called "Swingin' at the Madaville" it referred not only to the studio but it could've referred also to your home?
That's right.
Uh huh. You say you played only one concert -- public concert -- the whole time you were in England?
That's right.

Now I think you also had to, in order to renew your permission or residence permission or permission to stay in England, you had to move in and out of the country several times. How did that work out?

Well, I would only get a permit for a limited number of weeks or months and after which I would have to leave the country and then apply for a re-entry permit, which was always granted, fortunately -- but this gave me, you know, an excellent opportunity and reason to set up concerts on the Continent. You know. In other European countries. So that's how I managed to get to play in between.
Right. I'm not sure that we've got the date that you arrived in London. You got to Paris sometime in May of 1935.
Actually, I didn't get to Paris in
May. But I think I left for Paris in May.
Uh huh.
If my memory serves me correctly, because when I arrived at Cherbourg, where I disembarked and was to take the train, the boat train to Paris, I was confronted by the French police.
That's nice.

Yes, they had been told that I was a kidnapper. I had my daughter with me and I think if my memory serves me correctly, and the reports were correct, that the then Mrs. Carter -- the mother of my daughter --
What was your daughter's name, by the way?
Joyce.
This is Joyce.

Yes. Mrs. Carter had said that her daughter had been kidnapped by an unknown man, and I think that she had sworn out something that was known as a John Doe Warrant. But when the French police found out I was the father, they didn't, you know, respect such a law, that a father who took his child somewhere was a kidnapper. But to set the record straight and to you know, curtail any confusion that might arise later or any unpleasantness, I volunteered to take the next boat back to America.
You're kidding.
Which I did. I went back, and I was
met by police officers who took me to the Tombs. You've certainly heard of the Tombs in of New York.
Yes.

And I was bailed out by an attorney. Someone got me an attorney, and then when we finally went to court, the case was, of course, dismissed. It cost me quite a lot of money to take care of that little item. And as soon as the case was dismissed, as I remarked earlier, my dear friend, George Rifch, loaned me $150 so I could go back to my job in Paris.
Right. Yes.
Because by that time I was quite broke.
So you arrived a little bit later in Paris, and then you're going to London ... was how long after you arrived in Paris?
Well, I guess I went back to Paris at that point, it seems to me, it must have been about July -- some time in July.
Uh huh.
And then I know that I heard from Leonard Feather about the London situation about March.
Yes.
And I probably went to London within three months or something like that.
I think you actually went there in
March.
Oh really? Did I?
Yeah, I think -- now that I remember a little more clearly, the negotiations -- the letter from Leonard Feather came some time in February, I believe.
Oh, well, maybe that was it. Yeah.

Yeah. Because in the Melody Maker in February, the they reporters were already predicting, reporting that this discussion was going on and that you would probably come to England in the very near future, which I think you did. I think it was in March.
Probably then.
Or perhaps early April, at the latest, of 1936.
Uh huh.

Okay. Then, every time you had to leave Paris, or every time you had to leave London because of this visa arrangement, you did it -- was that the occasion for a tour in Europe each time, or did you sometimes go out of the country without a tour arranged?
Well, I suppose sometimes I did. But usually it was, you know, I knew when I was going to have to leave, and I would set up a series of concerts.
Right. Did you have a regular booking agent at that time, or how did that work?
Not a regular one, but I worked with a booking agent in London, in Holland, and Kyabons (PHONETIC) in Copenhagen.
Right. So these tours of the continent began how long after you got from ... you say you arrived in London, March-April of 1936.
Right.
When did you begin to go to the continent and either record, which you did, or play dates?
Maybe about July or so of that same year.
Which countries did you go to? Not necessarily in the order in which it took place, but just generally?
Well, I went back to France.
Did you play again with Willie Lewis?

No, I didn't play again with Willie Lewis, but I did play at a club in Paris with a group of my own at a club called the [Basil a Toit]-- and I also played in Holland at a place called the [Kerr House] Palace. I played there for 3 months. I believe that was the summer of '37.
Right.
And I played in Sweden and Denmark.
I think I played a 2 or 3 week engagement at the National [Schala] in Copenhagen. I played, you know, concerts around there.
And this was always with groups of local musicians from these countries, or were they also people that you took along from other places?

Well, actually, I took a band to -- when I went to Holland and played at Schala for 2 or 3 months, I took a band from England. It was quite an international band. Oh, I had a Jamaican player named Bertie Bernie King who played tenor saxophone, I think Louis Stevenson who played alto saxophone was from the British West Indies; I don't remember if he was from Trinidad or where; he wasn't Jamaican. I had ... gee, who else did I have? Yorke de Souza, I believe, on piano.
And they were all based in London?
They were all based in London, yes. I had an English player named Ray Webb on guitar; George Chisolm on trombone.
Yeah. And wasn't there a Ralph somebody at that time, I think, in that group?
No, there was a Cliff Wood Wildridge who played the other trumpet.
Uh huh.
Who played trumpet, and then there
was a lead trumpet player named Sam Dasburg, and he was ...
Yeah. Where was he from?
He was from Holland.
Uh huh.
He was the only local person we had up there.
What about ... there wasn't Freddie Williams in that band?
Who was Freddie Williams? You're thinking of Freddie Johnson.
Freddie Johnson, I'm sorry.
No. Freddie Johnson didn't play with me there. Freddie Johnson only recorded with me.
He recorded with you.
Yeah. Freddie Johnson and I never played together during my time in Europe, although we played together in the very early years at the dance palaces in New York.
Yes. You mentioned him a little earlier.
Yes.

How much was known in the public, in the Scandinavian countries, or even in Paris, about the kind of music -- the jazz that was being played then in America? And that I know it was now being exported, so to speak,
to these countries. Did they know a great deal about it? Were there very big audiences? Were they ...
Well, obviously, they did. They certainly knew me; they knew me much better than I had realized. I had what I might say was an interesting experience.

When I went to Copenhagen the first time, I went by boat from ... Fee, I don't know, from Dover or wherever the boats go to Esbjerg and then you take the boat train to Copenhagen ... but on this boat, a gentleman at that time -- Otto of Haasburg, you certainly know of him?
Yes. Yes.

He was very much in the news at that time. And I knew he was on board and of course, he was also aboard the boat train, and as we pulled in to the station in Copenhagen, the railroad station, that is -- there was, you know, I was standing on the corridor, you know how the European trains are.
Right.

I was standing in the corridor at the window, looking out and everybody -- there was quite a mob, so naturally, they were coming to meet -- this was a reception for the Haasburg, whom I found out later, was probably traveling incognito, I don't know.
But anyway, I was looking out the window, and all of a sudden, someone pointed to me and said something in

Danish, which probably was equivalent to "There he is!" -- you know? And this huge crowd, cheering went up, and I went to the door to get down out from the train, and I was literally lifted on to the shoulders of people ...
No kidding!

Yeah, and they carried me out of the station in to a waiting automobile and I was taken to my hotel with this crowd behind. And I was really never so thrilled, because I had not been there before, and Karl Kai Evans, who was the entrepeneur, and also a very fine musician, he was like the Paul Whiteman of, I guess we might say, Scandinavia, but especially of Denmark, and he had arranged these bookings for me, and it was a very, very wonderful reception. Yeah, he took me, I'll never forget it, he took me to the Hotel Nordland and had this great reception for me, and it was just wonderful.
So obviously, then, they knew you.
Yes.
And they knew about jazz and about American music.
Yes, they did.

To a considerable extent. But you must've at this time, while Swing and jazz were developing in America, you were really re-introducing it, in some sense, in Europe. In places where it had probably not
been for some years.

Yes, I guess so. I don't remember who had been to Scandinavia. I think maybe Armstrong had already been to Scandinavia, but I should think by '35, I think he had been. Ellington ... had Ellington been to Scandinavia?
I really don't know.
He'd certainly been to England, you know.
Yes.
But they were familiar with it, and they knew what it was all about.

Right. Then you -- at the end of these tours, you always went back to London and you made a number of recording sessions there with Vocalion I think, a new label, and Leonard Feather, I think, was involved in some of those.
Well, I think Leonard was involved in all of them.
All of those recordings.
Yes, he set them up, and he, I guess, was what you would call the producer.
Right. Did you try at that time to get them to relax the restriction against playing? Or did you sort of give that up after you saw the lay of the land?

Well, I guess I didn't work at it very hard. Uh huh. The band boy, too.

But you don't want to think about that.

Well, no. I think you're right. That's a good observation, and I agree. I think so. I think that something much more could have happened had there been someone sufficiently interested enough, to say, 'Well, gee, this thing deserves financing and maybe I can make some money out of it,' you know.
Yeah. It seems that you could never keep them together long enough to have them take with the public.
That's right.

Yes, yes. He was in the picture.

No, I didn't.
You played?
I played on the soundtrack.
Right. And some of those were issued as records later on?
Yes.
