Right. That was the second house.
That was the second house.
Well, where was that first house?

The first house, I think was on ... where was it? Gee, there were a couple of houses. I think there was one on Kenwood or something --- I'm not sure, as a matter of fact, for some reason I guess I'd rather forget that house. I only lived in that house for about 2 weeks. With myself.
Uh huh. And the second one was the one that ...
The second was on Hollyridge Drive in Hollywood, where I lived for 18 years.
Right. That was the one that you
That was the one that I said I was going to sell.
Oh, but you didn't.
Of course. I had no intention of selling, but I was just stalling for time to keep from spending money on legal fees and going in to Court for all of that, and ...
When this whole question would become, as the lawyers say, 'moot' with the Supreme Court decision.
Yes, that's right exactly.

Very good. Now, two more things. The brief one first. In the Time Life records recreation of the Swing Era, in a book they published, Milt Hinton is quoted as saying that "People don't know this, but Benny -- referring to you -- is responsible for the Musicians Credit Union. It's very hard for musicians to get loans, because they have nothing to give a bank as collateral. Benny confidently went to Local 802 and got them to set up a credit union, and he put in the first $18,000. That was 5 or 6 years ago -- and it's still going strong." Five or six years ago would have been, then, in about the mid 1960's. I'm not sure that this doesn't really relate to Hollywood very much perhaps, but he's talking about Local 802 which is in New York, isn't it?
Yes. But ... I'm a member.
You're still a member of that.
Oh yes, that was my first local, yes.
So what was that all about.

Oh, I don't know. I can't take any credit for setting up the credit union. I think ... well, I just made a deposit, you know, in the credit union, and I think I was maybe the first depositor, or something; I don't know. And that's all, you know.
All the exaggerations in our discussion are exaggerations that other people make of your role which you then reduce. You never increased the role that you played in anything.
Well, that's the way it is.

Okay. Now, the other thing that I wanted to ask you about -- there's much more that is related to Hollywood, and it goes back earlier, and I think that's in the early fifties, if I remember correctly, relating to the situation of the two segregated locals -- the black musicians local and the white local in Los Angeles. You came on the scene in the early 40's slowly, I suppose, you became more familiar with what was going on in the situation between the 2 unions, and you were a member of, of course, of the black local when you first had to join in Hollywood. What was the disadvantage of that segregated situation that led you and some others, I think, to become active in trying to overcome it? What was the disadvantage

Well, I think it's like any segregated situation where we're both supposedly members of the parent organization -- AFM -- American Federation of Musicians -- and in the local situations, there are two separate locals; one for white and one for black.

I think the feeling was at that time that the blacks were denied access to the good jobs and to the studios. As I said before, there were no blacks in the studios, with the exception of, of course, Lee Young, and I guess any other of us from studio to studio could even consider ourselves the token blacks at any given time, even when we were there just on one call. Usually, I was called when there were solos to be played, for which I was paid much above scale -- sometimes as much as 3 times scale, you know, which wasn't a lot of money for it, but was considerably more than I think -- $30 a session, at that time, in the very early days.
And of course, the indignity of being considered on the lower level, you know? And we thought we should get together and fight this and amalgamate the two locals and have just one union.
Who were some of the colleagues you were associated with in this movement to amalgamate?
Well, there were so many -- I wouldn't like to start naming names, because I wouldn't want to omit

any people who played important parts -- and so many people did, including many, many musicians. White musicians of good will, you know. Actually, we had petitions signed, and gee -- I think a couple of petitions I had signed, the first was signed, the first name on my petition was Alfred Newman, and gee, there were people like ... oh, there were just so many.

But I think, notably, I might mention Marl Young, who is the secretary of Local 47, now, and he is black, and he is a Chicago musician who also has a law degree. And he was the one who really worked very hard and drew up the proposals, under which we merged.

And if I am correct, I think the proposals that he drew up were so well done that they were just accepted in toto, or just as they were delivered, you know -- and Marl deserves a lot of credit. A lot of people say that Benny Carter was the one, but I feel it was Marl, and I always give the credit to him.
Well, of course, he gives a lot of credit to you.

Well, that's very nice. Probably the thing ... that I got around a little more than Marl and I made a little more records than Marl, and people knew my name better than they knew Marl Young's, but I feel that he was really the hard worker.
And do you feel that the situation

Yes, I think it's better; I think it's much better. Much better. And I think even the people who fought us in 767 --that was the black local -- to keep it black; you know, there were many blacks who didn't want the desegregation, you know?
Yes.
But even they had come around to, you know, feeling that this was a good thing.
Well, that's the ultimate testimony.
Yeah. Well, it's working very well. Working very well.

Well, we've come to a kind of period in the late 40's, you are working to some extent, in Hollywood in a variety of kinds of work; you don't have a regular band any more, but you put bands together every now and then, and take dates ... you are composing, recording, working in Hollywood; do you see this ...
Well, I'm not really composing yet. I'm writing songs.
No, you're writing songs. I know that. I meant that you were still writing music.
Right. Still writing music, indeed.
Right. And some beautiful tunes, you know. The records that you're making ... and then later

you do some special records with Count Basie and others and so on, for which you were composing a great deal. Also, your "Jazz Calendar, you made about half the tunes or so on that 12, monthly idols, if you can call them that.

Do you ... this of course, must have appeared to you as a very different mode of life from the one that you had led with your occasional bands in Europe, on the road and so on. Did that begin to give you more satisfaction in a personal way to lead a more ... or a less geographically mobile existence?

I guess so. I kind of felt a little like settling down and taking it a little easier, and I was becoming more interested, you know, as I went along in writing for films, as we had said before. And I wasn't satisfied with, you know, the sweet smell of failure, as I mentioned before -- but I was experiencing with the band -- we weren't really making a lot of money. Just doing all right, you know? But for all the work that was going in to it, it looked like we were never gonna get a hit record, and a hit record was really the thing that would really catapult you in to the Big Time, you know -- it was what you really needed.
And I just thought I'd stop fighting it.

Right. But did that give you some leisure to pursue other interests? You know, I know that you ... is that when you became interested in art and read more, I mean, when you had a more settled kind of existence?
I guess so. Yes, I got a little lazier.
Yes.
Uh ...

Let's touch on a number of things that you did for films. I won't worry about the dates or the order because these can be checked in various directories, you know, of film music, and by the way, let's talk about on TV, too. But I would like to mention some of these films, and get clear what your role was in one way or another. As examples of your work during the fifties, sixties, and down to the present.
Maybe perhaps, dealing a little bit with the earlier ones. Let's again, in no particular chronological order ... Pennies "The Five Pennies" -- you did something on that film.
I did some arranging, and it seems there was a sequence in there where there was ... someone portrayed Jimmy Dorsey.
Right.
And I played, you know, on the soundtrack on the background what Jimmy Dorsey was supposed to be playing in the picture.
Right. "An American in Paris."
"American in Paris" I did some arrangements on the film, and I had I think it was a sextette, on screen -- I suppose it was in a nightclub scene.
And that, I think, has been
repeated recently, or shown again in this ...
"That's Entertainment" number one, or part one, that is.
"The View from Pompeii's Head".
That was the same. Where I did some arranging on the picture, and I also had a small group, probably a sextet in a scene at a house party, I believe it was.
Yes. "Panic in the Streets".

"Panic in the Streets" I did well, quite a lot of writing on that, arranging, and there was an interesting thing about "Panic in the Streets". That was the first picture ... no, oh no ... am I thinking about "Panic in the Streets?" No, I was thinking about "No Way Out". But "Panic in the Streets", yes, I also wrote a little blues song for that picture. A thing called "No Good Man" that was sung in there by Helen Humes. Yes, that was Jack Palance.
How about "The Sun Also Rises".
"The Sun Also Rises" ... what did I do? I did some writing on that, and playing.
"Guns of Navarone".
Navarone I did some arranging with Dimitri Tiomkin.
Which reminds me, that we must get to Stanley Wilson, whom you were associated with considerably.
Yes.
I don't know ... were you associated with Stanley Wilson and Alfred Newman at the same time, or did one die -- did Alfred Newman die before you worked into your relationship with Stanley Wilson?
No. Actually ....
How did that work?
Actually, Alfred Newman, I believe -- now where are we? In 1976. I think Alfred Newman probably died about 1972, didn't he?
Did he die that recently?
Yes, actually -- but my association with Stanley Wilson didn't commence until about 1958.
Uh huh. How did that start?

Well, I was doing a thing with a friend of mine, Herman Herbert Stein, who was a composer at Universal Studios. He and Mancini had worked together quite a lot. We were working on a film ... I think it was, oh, what was it -- it must have been an M Squad (PROTOTYPE); it was a segment of something, and he had me over to do some solo saxophone bit in it.
That was the film, "M Squad" -- is that what you were saying?
Yes.
Not the TV show.
Well, was there a film, "M Squad"?
I think there was.
Well, maybe. I don't know. Either that,
or was it a segment of 'M Squad' or a segment of something else.
That was on TV ... there was a TV show called 'M Squad'.
If it was 'M Squad', now I'm not sure.
Oh, I'm sorry.
But it was a segment of something.
Right.

And Herman had done it as a composer and Stanley Wilson was the music head, and after we finished doing this, and I had met Stanley. he asked me if I'd be interested in doing composition on 'M Squad,' you know ... doing a segment.
This is the TV show.
The TV? Well, was there a picture called 'M Squad?'
I don't know.
I don't think so.
I don't think so. Stanley Wilson, at that time, asked you in his capacity as head of music for Universal?
That's right.
I see.
Yes. And if I would be interested in, you know, doing an 'M Squad' segment. And I said yes. So I did one, after which they asked me if I would like to do another ... finish the series.
Uh huh. So that was your
introduction to TV?

To TV and to composition. Because prior to that, I'd only done arranging and orchestrating. And then with doing TV, which meant that I had to do all of the background, you know, the underscoring of everything that was done. In essence, when I started doing it, then it was my picture, my responsibility completely.
Right. And that was the beginning of that phase of your Hollywood career?
That's right.
Uh huh. And then you had a lot to do with Stanley Wilson in his capacity as Universal head; music, both in films and in TV.
Well, actually, I never did a film at Universal.
Oh, I see.
Not a full film ... not a theatrical film.
Oh, I see.
I'd done one project, [Four and Twenty] (PHONETIC) which is like ... that's a two hour show, but it's still for TV, and that differs in category from a theatrical film.
Right. And then you did some records with -- some recording, I think, with Stanley Wilson.
Yes ... yes.
Right.
How long ago did he die?
It seems he died in 1970, I believe.
Uh huh. Let me go back to your work in one film in the early 50's, "The Snows of Kilimanjaro". Do you recall what you did there?

Yes. Well, I appeared in the film as, you know, a saxophone soloist. I did some writing; I don't remember the extent of it now, but it was just some, you know, arranging. That was ... let's see, was that Hugo Friedhofer or was it Bernie Herman's picture.
I think that was Bernard Herman.
Bernard Herman's picture, yes. Uh huh.
It was 20th Century Fox.
Yes, that's right.
A lot of people ... several people have written about that blues that you played in that film. You know, when Gregory Peck and ...what's her name ...
Ava Gardner.
... Ava Gardner were in a nightclub scene or something, in Paris, was it?
Yes, I believe so.
What were you playing there?
Well, that was a song written by Alfred Newman, that at the time he called "Love is Cynthia" or did he change the title. It was called at one time, "Blue
Mountain" -- and then we recorded it once later in an album, and he called "To Ava" ...
Yes.
So it's had 3 titles.
What about "The Hanged One" ... in that film?
You mean "The Hanged Man".
"The Hanged Man", yes.
That was -- that's right, well, that was still a film for TV, wasn't it -- at Universal? Yes, I did that.
You did the background?
Yes. I did the complete picture, yes.
Who was in that?
Oh, Broderick Crawford ... I think, Robert Culp, Vera Miles.
Uh huh. Where did, or how did your tune, "Only Trust Your Heart" get written? Did that have to do first with a TV show, or ...
Yes, that was for a TV show ... what was that? Was that over at 20th?
"It Takes a Thief" or "Fame is the Name" or something.
Oh no, that came from "The Hanged Man".
"The Hanged Man".
Yeah, that came from the "Hanged Man", yes.
Was Astrud Gilberto in that?
In a nightclub scene, with the Stan Getz quartet.
I see.
Yes, that's right. And following that, they recorded it.
And she just appeared -- she was not a character in the story, was she?
No, no. She just appeared as a singer in the club.
Uh huh.
An interesting thing about that song, "Only Trust Your Heart" -- I don't know that I've told you about that before, but Sammy Cahn wrote the lyrics to that song.
Yes.

And when the first record came out in the album, it listed as composer Nicholas Bronsky, Nicholas Bronsky and Sammy Cahn -- and when I saw this, I got in touch immediately with the studio, and wanted to know what had happened here. And I was told that they didn't really know, but that they would look into it.
Well, they got back to me, and what they discovered

was that Sammy Cahn has, inadvertently, of course, written, or used the same title that he had used for another song, with which, you know, that he had collaborated with Nicholas Bronsky on. And I don't know how labeling or programming or whoever the people at the record company could have gotten his name on it, because they would certainly have received the music, you know, from my own song. I would think so -- or maybe they just took the title and just looked it up in the ASCAP files or something and said, "Well, Bronsky and Cahn".

But Sammy had forgotten that he had written another song by this title. Noe he's a very prolific writer, as we know -- but the funny thing about it was I dismissed it then; I said, "Well, it's probably some little insignificant song that they wrote" -- and never did anything with more.

And then just a few months ago, I was looking at late television and I don't know why I happened to look at a picture called "Ten Thousand Bedrooms" with Dean Martin -- and here's this song, "Only Trust Your Heart". But of course, it's the Nicholas Bronsky melody, and the other Sammy Cahn lyric. But the only thing that's the same about our song is the title.
Is the lyric on the same theme?
I don't remember the lyric, because I don't even remember what the song sounded like. As a matter of fact, I think that what happened, if I heard the song, I
probably didn't hear it sung --but in the credits at the end, I saw the song, "Only Trust Your Heart" by Nicholas Bronsky and Sammy Cahn. And I said, "Ah, that's it!"
Well, there's a lot of repetition in these things, but also I didn't realize in the titles, even.
Well, I have two songs called "Once Upon a Time".
That's right.

But the second one is called "Once Upon a Time It Happened " -- and that was because the lyricist, you know, wrote -- used that title for the song, not knowing that I had another song called "Once Upon a Time" --and Dean Martin liked the song, and recorded it.
Does Ed know that -- about his recording of it?
Oh, I think so. Yes.
Oh, he must.
Yes.
Well, I want to ask you about "The Flower Drum Song".
Yes?
Do you remember what you did there?
I didn't do a great deal. I did some arranging, some orchestrating, and I played in the orchestra.
Okay. Now on TV, your first work
Yes.
But you also worked on "The Bold Ones"
I did a couple of segments. Yes.
By a 'segment' you mean you did a couple of episodes.
Episodes, yes, that's right.
"Ironside".
Yes, a number.
Now what did you do with "Night Gallery"?
I did a couple of segments of that.
Was that a serial, I mean, something that went on week after week?
Yeah, with Rod Serling staying, (unintelligible).
Then the "Pearl Bailey Show" -- that was the recent show that she was on? She had a regular series about 3 years ago, was it?
Oh, maybe a little longer -- about '71-, '72. I guess.
Uh huh. And you did, not the ...
I did the arrangements.
Just the arrangements of particular tunes that she sang when the band played.
Right, uh huh.
Was there something called a "Markam"? Did you do a "Markam"?
"Markam" was a TV show at Universal, I probably did a segment of that.
Right. Do you find any difference between TV and ... what would you call them, theatrical films, or something?
No drastic difference, no.
Essentially, the technique and the work is the same.
The mechanics are pretty much the same.
You have a little bit more time with a theatrical film, or, you know, because it's a big studio, bigger band, usually.
Usually, yes.
And a bigger budget.
Yes. Oh yes.
And a little bit more time to work on it, but otherwise, the mechanics are pretty much ...
Yes, the mechanics are pretty much the same.

Uh huh. We talked earlier about the very few black musicians and composers working in Hollywood, and in the early 40's when you came. That, of course, has changed somewhat. I mean, there are some more.
Yes, it's changed quite a bit.
Who are some of those people who have come since your time ... since your first ...

Well, I guess notably, Quincy Jones; that's the first one the pops into my mind. First name. Gee, Quincy ... I don't know when he came; he did "The Pawnbroker" -- I don't know what year that was. But up to now, he's done over 30 films, you know.
Uh huh.
Oliver Nelson has done a few films, and a great number of TV shows.
JJ. Johnson has ...

JJ. Johnson has ... actually, JJ. Johnson is now doing "The Six Million Dollar Man" which, you know ... he has taken over on that. After Oliver Nelson passed away. Last year. And Benny Golson, we must remember, too.

And you saw all these people coming in? I mean, they came in while you were there. Did they -- did their work begin with one film, usually -- how did they break in? I mean, what was the process? Did they come there for one particular purpose -- with a contract already in their hands, or did they just come there and say, well, "Here I am. I'm gonna try to get some work in the studios."?
Well, I don't know about the others, but I know how Oliver Nelson came there, and I don't want to give any undue credit to myself, because it's not

why I'm telling you this, but when I was working at Universal, I was asked to look at a picture for a producer, and I looked at the picture and he said that he wanted a score like an album that he was going to play for me. And he played an album for me, and it was, I believe it was a Jimmy Smith album, that had been done by Oliver Nelson.

So he wanted this kind of music -- wanted to know could I do this. Well, at the time, I was very, very busy anyway, doing other things, and I would have kind of had to cram to get that in my then busy schedule.

So I knew that they had, you know, brought composers from as far away as Paris and London to do just a TV episode, you know? And I said, 'Well, gee, this is done by Oliver Nelson --why don't you try to get him to come and do this segment for you. When does it have to be done? If this is the music that you really want; if it's that important to you, get the man who does it so well.' You know.
: Sure.
And so they thought this was a good idea, but wanted to know did I think he would come. I said, 'Well, all you can do is contact him.'
And I helped him get in touch with him, and Oliver agreed to come and do it, and once he came, they liked his work.
: And he liked it.
And he liked it, and that was it.
But of course that's just one particular case.

That's one particular case, but of course I know that Neal Hefty was invited out there under somewhat similar circumstances, not by any instigation of mine, but I know Dick Klein was telling me that when, I believe it was "Sex and the Single Girl" ... he wanted that sound that Hefty had been getting, you know, with the Basie thing, and he just picked up a phone one day and called Neal Hefty in New York, and said, "How would you like to come out and work on a picture for me?" It was just like that, and he came -- and you know, he did quite a succession of things, following that.
The Hollywood work goes on and off; I mean, it isn't something like a band where you're doing something every day and it's just a question of getting an assignment, so all this time ...
(CUT)

... all right, Benny, I want to continue with you now, summarizing this varied period of the 50's and 60's, which is so different from your career in the late 20's and the 30's and 40's. We tend to think in these decades, but of course, they overlap a bit.
Now you do, in the 50's, a variety of things, as I mentioned earlier, including records, albums with these

groups that you pick up for various purposes. They tend to be musicians more on the West Coast now than on the East Coast. There's a long period of time when you don't play on the East Coast, except later at the Newport Jazz Festivals, but for a long time, you're not appearing on the East Coast at all. Isn't that true?
Yes, that is quite true.
Uh huh. Did you miss New York?
Not really.
You liked it out there.
Yes, I liked living in California, and when I go to New York, it's always something I look forward to, and as soon as I get there, I'm ready to leave.
Certainly by the time you've finished, anyway.

Certainly, yes. I always say I'm gonna stay a few days, you know, longer, but I don't really have any real desire once I spend a little time there. I haven't spent much time playing there in the last few years, although I was there, I think, oh, a couple of times -- probably once in '62 and once in '65, just conducting the show for Peggy Lee.
Right.
... during which I didn't play at all, you know?
Right. It's around that time, too,
that you made one or two albums for Impulse, and for a long time after that, you didn't make an album. Those were the "Further Definitions" and "Additions to Further Definitions."
Right.
And in the first one, you -- what was the theme or the motif of the further definitions?
Well, as Bob Thiele
Field?

Field, mentioned to me -- he'd like me to, you know, just use the saxophone section and recreate a couple of things that Coleman Hawkins and I had done in Paris many years earlier with the two French saxophone players, Andre Ekyan, the altoist, and Alex Combelle, who is a tenor saxophone player; so we got together, oh, Phil Woods on the other alto and Charlie Rouse on the other tenor, Coleman Hawkins, myself -- with Jimmy Garrison on base and Dick Katz on piano, and Joe Jones on drums and John Collins on guitar, just with the 8 piece group, we made that "Further Definitions."
And you did a few of the tunes of those famous brase.
Yeah, "Crazy Rhythm" and "Honeysuckle Rose" ... and we did some other things.
Uh huh. Then you did an "Additions" to Further Definitions.
Yes.
And do you ... was there any special
reason why you didn't do any albums after the second of these two?
The only special reason was that nobody asked me! So I suppose that's good enough unless I wanted to so some myself, which I kept saying I was going to do, but never got around to it.
Uh huh. But you were very busy; you were doing a lot of things .... traveling.
Yes ... busy doing things for other people and traveling.
Touring ...
Yes.
Tours of Europe, tours of ...
when did you first go to Japan, by the way?
I believe that was 1953 or '54.
That early?
Yes ... with Norman Granz's Jazz at the Philharmonic.
Uh huh. And then?
Then I returned in 1973, which was like 20 years later, and now I'm going again this coming April, '77.
Uh huh. But as things developed, of course, in the late 60's, you began a kind of a different type of date, playing at colleges and universities. I don't mean on a regular basis, but ...
Yes.
But you began to develop an interest in this kind of .. and also in teaching.
Yes.
Where did that begin?
Well, that began with an invitation from a gentleman from Princeton University, a Dr. Monroe Berger, whom I'm sure you've met.
Yes. Coming and going.

Coming and going, yes. And I hadn't met him, and I didn't know him, and he said if I was interested, he would come out to California at some future period and talk about it with me. And much to my surprise, he really came!

And we talked about it, and it wound up with my coming to Baldwin Wallace College, I believe that was in Middleburg, just outside of Cleveland. Berea, Ohio. And it seems that Mr., or Dr. Berger, who was doing these things, had been asked to come to Baldwin Wallace and he asked them if he could invite me. As a matter of fact, I don't know whether he made it one of the conditions or not, but I was very, very flattered and honored, and of course, quite pleased.
Was that the first time, then, that, you know, you spend the week there ...
Yes.
And then you played at some concerts; the Illinois Jazz Band with ...
Yes ... with John Garvey and his band came, yes.
And you would do a concert with them and you would do a concert with a trio from Cleveland.
Right.

Then you also met in workshops with students and talked with groups of students. Was that the first time that you had any extended contact -- extended at least, over a week's time ... with college students?
Yes. That was really I'd done anything of that nature, really.
Did you feel that that was something worthwhile doing? Was it an important thing to you? Was it some new dimension that you welcomed?
It was very, very new to me, of course, and very rewarding. I enjoyed it very much and it just really stimulated my interest in doing it more.
It was interesting also because students by and large were no longer jazz oriented; they were quite rock oriented at that time ...
Right.
Well how did ... you must have expected that, of course?

Well, I did expect it, but I was very pleased to see that the students, you know, that were getting in to their upper teens and beyond, were really getting much more interested -- and knowledgeable -- about jazz, you know? Which I found to be on a continued basis, even later, after I came to Princeton for a semester. And even after leaving Baldwin Wallace and coming to Princeton, I believe, for about a week or a couple of days here, ...
Right, and that was in early 1970?
Yes.
Directly after Baldwin Wallace.
Yes, that's right. After Baldwin Wallace. And it was very, very interesting -- the reaction of the students, and I guess I hadn't expected to find as much interest in jazz as I did.
You found more than you anticipated?
Yes, I think I did.
Well, did you find a knowledge of music that surprised you?
Oh, yes.
... that the kids were technically proficient?
Yes.
Even if the music was not jazz or if it was rock oriented?
Yes; they were being well schooled.

And of course when you came to Princeton, which was right after leaving Baldwin Wallace, we had a seminar with some jazz historians and critics of various times, including people like Dan Morganstern and Billy Taylor -- these were several that we did ...
Willie Ruff ...
Willie Ruff was here, Larry Ridley, and ...
Yes, that's right ... from Rutgers.
So this now became a combination of seminars, chats, workshops, and then concerts, all at the same time,
Yes, yes.
But this kind of variety -- did it prove for you to be particularly welcome?
Oh yes, indeed. Very.

Just to refresh your memory, you got an invitation from Princeton from the Afro American Studies and Program of the Council of Humanities to come for a semester, and that was the Fall semester of 1973.
Yes, that's right.
What were your ideas about what you ought to be doing at that time, and what did you do?
Well, prior to coming, I wasn't sure what I was going to be doing, but I was, you know, very pleased

that you allowed me the freedom to just come and really establish my own program, so to speak. I mean, because I didn't know what I was going to do; I had no sort of degree -- honorary or otherwise -- and I'd had just a small measure of formal training, and I had neither the time nor the inclination, and maybe not even the knowhow, I must add, to structure a curriculum.

of the chord, the way they voiced here in closed position. So I mean, does that sound like some sort of a general description of what's going on -- at least in this ...
In general.
Okay.

In General, but I don't know what it means! I don't know what it means to the listener ... I guess maybe we're talking for the music student rather than for the listener who probably couldn't care less, other than it's pleasing to the ear.
Okay.
I ... I ... but for the music student, we could go further, if you'd like.
Please comment.

Well, you just said it. I don't know what else to say. I don't quite know what else to add, and I'm talking slowly because I am looking at this as I talk. No, I think you've explained it quite well. Even better than I could.

Let me ask something else, too, about what we might just put under the heading of 'repertoire'. What factors at various times in your career -- let's perhaps limit it to the question of your jazz work or what we'll call your jazz work, as unhappy as you are with that term, but it doesn't matter ...
Well, I'm not really unhappy with it. I just find it very limiting, yeah ...
imprecise.
Yeah. Imprecise is good enough.

But lacking a better term, at various stages of your career, how did you go about choosing a repertoire? That is, the music which was going to appear under your own name? I'm not talking about for hire work you did for other people -- but in your own bands, or -- especially in your own bands, what factors would have guided your choice of a repertoire, that is, the circumstances, or just what kinds of judgments?
You mean the sounds that I would select or something that I would write?
Well, both. I'm thinking more of a larger body of material that you put together, say, in a single evening, or over a certain period of time.
Just a song I would like, you know. I mean, you want to know how I -- on the basis of what would I choose a song I would like, or ...
Yeah ... or how you put together a body of material, what considerations? I mean, fast, slow?
Oh, you mean in a program?
Uh huh. In effect.
Uh huh, in effect. Well, naturally, I think it would -- I would take in to consideration the matter
of pacing, you know, which I think is always something we think of in programming something -- one thing too similar doesn't follow another thing, you know.
Right.
Right.

But I was -- I'm sort of getting at sort of a larger perspective of maybe a larger body of work here, and I don't know if these observations -- if you agree with these or not, but in looking at, say, your work from the 1930's as a general enough statement right there, that in the things that you would offer under your own name -- Benny Carter and his orchestra -- and there are a couple of generalizations that might be made about just the material you presented under your own name.
There's very little blues, for example. Is that a reasonable generalization? Or relative to what other people might have been doing at that time?
No, I guess I just didn't think along those terms, too much. You know what I mean? What did I do in the way of blues -- I did some blues. Not too many, though, did I?
Not ...
"D Blues" -- that was with the Chocolate Dandies. "Big Ben Blues" in England. What else did I do in blues? "Blues in My Heart" which was really not the blues.
I can't recall anything else, can you? : Not off hand. I'm really groping around.
Yeah. So am I! No ... I don't know.

Well, there's another category, too, that --there is another technique that I have given a name to; I'm not going to launch it to that, but that is in which chord progressions were borrowed and then the original melody of that song, or whatever was discarded, and then the jazz arranger would put his own melody to that, borrowed set of chord progressions.
This is something else that it seems to me that you didn't do very much of; in fact, I'm really groping around for examples of that in this period.
I don't think anybody did much of that, did they, before Charlie Parker, I mean, you know?
Well, there was actually ... I mean, Duke did quite a bit of it himself; I mean, he ...

Well, the only instance I can recall is "Rose Room" which became In a Mellow Tone, and I think da da dee da ... what's the name of that? "I Let a Song Out of My Heart"? I understand that came from a lick that saxaphones played to "Once in Awhile"? Is that right?
Umm ... that could be. Uh huh.
Da, doo da da da and da doo dee dee... what else?
Well, there's a number of -- even a number of Ellington pieces.
That's what I mean. What other Ellington's can you ...
A little "Tiger Rag" ... lots of "Tiger Rag" pieces.
Oh, yes ... well, yes.
When the melody was discarded.
Yes. I don't know too many of those, though. Especially by other people, I don't know of any of them.
I don't have a list here, but the Missourians was another group that did a number of those.
Is that right?
Those "Tiger Rag" things -- [the Ozark Mountain groups] and so forth.
Taken from what?
From the chord progressions of "Tiger Rag."
Oh, yes. "Tiger Rag," yeah. Well ...
Well, the Basie band then, with a lot of "I Got Rhythm" ...
Oh yes.
But in general, I mean, is it ...
I even use an "I Got Rhythm" bridge in
a thing of mine called "Pom Pom".
Indeed. That's what? 1940?
Yeah. I mean, it had the "I Got Rhythm" chord structure. You know, and ... of course, I think the "I Got Rhythm" introductory melody first came from something by William Grant Still.
This has been claimed from the Afro American Symphony." This is what some people claim they say.
Yeah, the symphony ...
But I've gone through the score, and I can't find much on it.

Well, maybe it's not the Afro American Symphony." I think it's something earlier than that. And I think it's ... let me see, I can't remember the name of it, but I heard it. I heard it at something played by the Houston Symphony Orchestra when they played a thing -- a TV program, oh, I can't remember the title of it, but I wrote it down somewhere at home.
But in general, I think it's safe to say ...
But what I'm talking about is the part that says, da da da da, dee dee dee ... that's the part I'm talking about.
In the bridge ... at the end of the bridge.
No, not in the bridge. The melody. The da da da ... I got rhythm, da da da ... that's a William Grant Still thing. Definitely. Very definitely.
Okay. Well, I'll await your reference to that.
No, now I didn't mean the bridge on that. No.
Because the bridge in that case ... I mean, there are other songs even earlier than "I Got Rhythm" that had the same chord structure in the bridge, that's right.
Yes, that is right.
But in general, is it a fair statement to say that this is a technique of composing or arranging which you indulged very little? This kind of borrowed chord progression.
Well, I guess maybe I didn't. Maybe I should have.

Because it strikes me, in listening to these things -- well, comparing them, too, to a lot of other people active in various times. But there's a great deal of original material in your work, and maybe not even so many popular songs of the time as there is in other band leaders repertoires.
Never thought of it. Silly of me, wasn't it? Or negligent. Which?

Let me ask another one along those lines, and that is, how well -- let's stick to your case. To the recordings that survive, represent what actually transpired night by night by night? Is that an accurate document of the kind of music in terms of selections or the way it was played in live performances?
What do you mean, "night by night by night"?
Well, in your live performances, just as you were working to live audiences. Did the recordings pretty much reflect the same material?

Well, much of the studd that I hear today that I did in the earlier years, I just abhor. I absolutely hate it. I hate to listen to them, and some of the things that were done at tempoes that I, you know -- if I were to do those same arrangements today, I probably would cut the tempos, almost, in half.
Well, would you have played them for dancers or for a live audience or in a studio?
Well, I think that at the Savoy, I played a lot of things much faster for the Lindy Hop dances.
Uh huh.
You know they had ... we played opposite the Savoy Sultans, which was a great jump band, you know? They had tempos that you could not compete with. Don't ever be on

the other bandstand when the Savoy Sultans and play their tempos. You either had to play something slower or faster. Because they had a groove that you just -- you know, there was nothing else like it, with Razz Mitchell on drums, and Mike Kerr on bass, and gee, it was just a beautiful band, just a beautiful band; Al Cooper and the Savoy Sultans.

But they played for one type of thing, and we played for another type, and we were so often asked to play something fast, you know? We got into the habit of playing things at a tempo that, you know, what they called the "Lindy Hop" tempo, and ...
What about the time constrictions on 78 RPM recordings? How long would a performance; a live performance last? Typically or atypically?
Oh, I think there was, in the earlier days, before they got so concerned about the disc jockeys -- the time element, I think there was no worry about going over the 2 minute 58 or 3 minute ...
What about in live performances as compared with recording?
Oh, live performances? I don't remember that we had any particular restrictions.
So those would tend to be much longer?
Yes.
Much longer.
Yes, they could be. You know. And But not necessarily, but they could be.

Okay. I want to perhaps shift gears again here, and I'm not quite sure how to approach this in a sensible way, but I know there's a great deal of snobbery, I think, which is couched in the opposition of two words, as they are often used to try to describe music or make some point about different kinds of music, and that is "serious" and "popular" music. Do you think this makes any sense? I mean, is there something -- do you think this is a phony issue? I mean it's something that ... a lot of music simply gets, you know, consigned to -- the trashy by calling it "popular" whatever that means; I mean, it's more than a descriptive term the way a lot of people use it.

Well, it's hard again there to explain about the term, because it probably isn't as confusing a term as the term "jazz" --but it's probably just as phony as the term. And I think "jazz" at this stage is phony -- it's a phony term. It doesn't mean anything, The name thing, you know. And as I said before, you know, from Buddy Bolden to Chick Corea, you know, and you're talking about two different kettle of fish.

Well, let me maybe go at it like this. I don't know if you've been asked this question before, but you've done a lot of music for hire, in effect; that is, for lack of a more precise term, I'll call it commercial music; that is, music for film, for television,

etc. -- or arrangements for other bands, for which there are certain musical specifications. And I'm not sure if this question is gonna make much sense, but if you were gonna do something strictly for yourself and not have any kind of constraints; I mean, that is, you could use all the different kinds of instruments as you wanted, as many musicians or as few musicians as you liked, no time restraints, no financial restraints -- what would you do, or is this, maybe a silly question?

It is not a silly question. It's a very good question, Jim. It's a very good question particularly at this moment. Because I've just been talking about my next album or two that I'm going to do for Norman Granz for Pablo. And Norman has given me carte blanche do do anything I want to do. Now when I say "Anything" I want to do," you know, go and write or hire as many musicians as you want to, and this is probably for one or two albums.

Now the difficulty here with me is that it's a matter of making a decision. What do I want to do, you know? And you always feel like, gee, if I could only do just that what you really wanted to do, how would you go about it, what would you do? Of course, I'm doing one album coming up that I'm going to be doing with Ray Bryant -- it's just a quartet album, but then following that, I'll be doing an album with a big band, a number of men of my choice, the type of music of my choice, the composition of my choice -- my own or something else, you know.
And it's not like I had unlimited funds at my disposal and I wanted to go and do something for myself at my own financial risk, and I might then say see, well, gee, I might make 6 albums.
Uh huh.
Then, you know, I wouldn't have to worry so much about what am I going to do with this one album.
I see.

You know, I could do a series of different things, but I know that at least I can do one album now with no restrictions; no limitations, which of course, I don't intend to abuse -- I don't want to do anything on an ego trip and say, well, gee, you know, I can do anything I want -- let's go out and get 100 men, or, you know, hire the L.A. Symphony, and ... something like that.
But I'm not sure what I'm going to do. I'm really doing a lot of thinking about it at this moment.

Because I just wonder ... you know, about that, that is, if they quote, a "serious" musician sits down, a lot of things that are specified for the commercial musician, how long it is, how many instruments, are all compositional decisions, that this "serious" musician has to make for himself. For the commercial musicians, these decisions have been made for him, in effect.
Well, in this particular instance, I
I have to make this decision for myself, and as much as I wanted it, I would really like to have some direction, you know?
Right.

I guess maybe I want someone to share the responsibility. You know, maybe that's it, because I said to Norman, I said, I know that jazz records don't sell a million to begin with -- maybe with some exceptions; I understand that George Benson has a big exception right of as of this moment -- but I would like to think if you're going to invest a lot of money in an album, I would like to hope that -- because jazz records don't sell a lot instantly, but they do sell forever.
Uh huh.

You know? I'd like to feel that at least, in your lifetime, if not in mine, you'll be able to recover your investment. You know. So he laughed and he wasn't too worried about that. He's not too profit motivated. He does so many things for his own pleasure. So I'm going ahead and get started on this in the next few days.
Well, what kind of things are going through your mind now, as you do this? He says, go ahead and do what you want.
Yeah.
Well, are you starting with
practical considerations? How many musicians should I use, or are you thinking more in terms of ...
I'm thinking more in terms of at this moment of material.
Uh huh.

And of my own playing, you know, because I want to be in a good ... well, what is it I want to say? I want to be as well up on the instrument as I can be, and when I sit down and write, you know, I've got to think also if I'm gonna write maybe 6 hours a day, I better put aside 2 hours a day to practice, if I'm not playing in a club or something. You know, I've got to play the instruments, too.

Well, what is that like? That is, we hear about somebody like Duke Ellington, for example, so able to write for certain musicians. What's it like to write for yourself if you're the featured musician?
Well, the thing is, Duke Ellington wasn't too much a featured musician.
That's right.

He was, as he called himself, 'I'm just the piano player!' -- and Duke, as we know, was no slouch as a piano player, but he did write for the musicians and he always knew for whom he was writing -- he could be writing for Lawrence or for Johnny or for Coote for Carney or for Poole or for Kearney, you know. What's it like to be writing for myself? I would like

That's part of the decision, too --what I'm gonna play, you know. I would like to do something in the nature of a suite for a saxophone or, what you might call a concerto or something, you know -- something that wouldn't be too challenging technically, because I don't know how much practice time I'm gonna be able to put in, you know?
But I don't want to do anything to attempt to just display my ... what's the term I want to use?
Virtuosity or ...
Well, I was trying to shy away from that word, because I ...
Artistry, then.

All right. Artistry, you know, is good. But I'd like to do something that might also be an artistic success for me, and maybe, and very happily, a commercial success, you know, for the sponsor. I would like the audience to have -- I mean for the album to have reasonably fair audience appeal.

Uh huh. So that's a consideration, which a lot of people, I think, or a lot of, let's say, academic people types wouldn't consider maybe a compositional decision, but I don't see why not, I mean, that's -- indeed, that is a compositional decision.
Well, it is for me.
Yeah.
So if I can get over that hurdle, I can sit down and write. Like somebody will say, 'Shut up and deal!'
Okay. Benny, I think that provides a place for us to conclude.
Oh, to conclude? Good.
Okay. Very good. Thanks very much.
Thank you, Jim.
